title: Data and code for collision-model Dicke-state preparation: depth-fidelity frontiers, circuit costs, and superconducting-processor measurements
abstract: Dicke states are multipartite entangled states in which a fixed number of quantum excitations is coherently shared among many qubits. Originally introduced in the context of cooperative emission and superradiance, they are now important resources for quantum sensing, networking, and collective quantum phenomena. Preparing prescribed Dicke states with high fidelity, however, remains challenging, particularly as the system size and excitation number increase. Here we present an open dataset and accompanying code for preparing Dicke states using a collision-based quantum protocol. The dataset covers systems from five to fourteen qubits over a broad range of excitation numbers and records how the best-found noiseless preparation fidelity changes with circuit depth. It also provides circuit-resource estimates and experimental measurements for selected states on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald superconducting processor. The accompanying code reproduces the processed data and validation checks, providing a reusable benchmark for studying the trade-off between state-preparation fidelity, circuit cost, and hardware noise.
one_liner: Open data and code benchmark collision-model Dicke-state preparation up to 14 qubits, including IQM Emerald measurements.
why_it_matters: Dicke states are useful for sensing and networking, and this gives reproducible depth-fidelity and hardware-noise data for practical preparation tradeoffs.
detailed_summary: The work releases an open dataset and code for collision-based preparation of Dicke states from 5 to 14 qubits across multiple excitation numbers. It tracks best-found noiseless fidelity versus circuit depth, adds circuit-resource estimates, and includes selected measurements on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald superconducting processor. The dataset is framed as a reusable benchmark for separating algorithmic preparation limits from hardware noise effects.
main_result: The paper provides reproducible depth-fidelity frontiers, circuit costs, and selected 54-qubit-processor measurements for Dicke-state preparation.
application_angle: It supports hardware-aware preparation of multipartite entangled resources for quantum sensing, networking, and collective-state experiments.

title: SpiderLS: Leveraging Full ZX Reduction for Lattice Surgery Compilation
abstract: Lattice surgery compilation plays a central role in translating fault-tolerant quantum programs into efficient surface code realizations, where both spatial and temporal resources directly determine the cost of execution. Recent work has demonstrated the benefits of using ZX-diagrams as an intermediate representation for lattice surgery compilation, enabling semantics-preserving transformations that reduce spacetime cost. However, existing compilation restricts ZX reduction to preserve diagram structures that can be directly embedded as lattice surgery junctions. We present SpiderLS, which extends prior approach by leveraging full ZX reduction. To translate the resulting diagram into executable lattice surgery operations, SpiderLS applies a sequence of compiler passes that derives an execution order, generates target code by grouping compatible interactions into multi-target operations, and lowers the target code to Pauli-product measurements. The resulting explicit patch and Pauli-boundary requirements guide logical scheduling and structure-aware spacetime routing. Across representative algorithmic and random workloads, SpiderLS achieves average reductions of 49.2% in spacetime volume and 99.8% in compilation time compared with the prior ZX-based compiler.
one_liner: SpiderLS uses full ZX reduction to compile lattice-surgery circuits with much lower spacetime volume and faster compilation.
why_it_matters: Surface-code resource costs dominate fault-tolerant execution, so large reductions in spacetime volume directly affect feasible quantum hardware workloads.
detailed_summary: SpiderLS extends ZX-based lattice-surgery compilation by allowing full ZX reduction rather than preserving only directly embeddable junction structure. It then derives execution order, groups compatible interactions into multi-target operations, and lowers target code to Pauli-product measurements with explicit patch and Pauli-boundary requirements. Across representative and random workloads, it reports 49.2% average spacetime-volume reduction and 99.8% compilation-time reduction relative to a prior ZX-based compiler.
main_result: The demonstrated capability is full-ZX-reduction-based lattice-surgery compilation with substantially reduced spacetime volume and compilation time.
application_angle: It is directly relevant to making fault-tolerant quantum programs cheaper to schedule and route on surface-code hardware.

title: Efficient biphoton generation by a waveguide-coupled single atom
abstract: A single atom undergoing spontaneous four-wave mixing near a chiral waveguide can efficiently channel an emitted Stokes-anti-Stokes photon pair into two tightly confined waveguide modes, yielding thus enhanced biphoton generation without requiring loss suppression or stringent phase matching. We develop a perturbative treatment, valid for a four-level atomic system under experimentally realistic conditions, to explain physical origins and clarify relevant constraints of such an enhancement determined by the interplay of atomic decay rates toward guided and unguided modes. Besides achieving optimal generation rates equivalent to a cold atomic ensemble hundreds of micrometers long in free space, our biphoton source naturally fulfills key requirements for next-generation on-chip quantum light sources, namely low-loss operation, robustness, compactness, and scalability.
one_liner: A theory proposal shows efficient Stokes-anti-Stokes biphoton generation from a single atom coupled to a chiral waveguide.
why_it_matters: It points to compact, phase-matching-free on-chip photon-pair sources with rates comparable to much larger free-space atomic ensembles.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a perturbative treatment of spontaneous four-wave mixing in a four-level atom near a chiral waveguide. The mechanism channels Stokes and anti-Stokes photons into tightly confined guided modes, with enhancement set by the balance of guided and unguided decay rates. Under realistic conditions, the predicted generation rate can match that of a cold atomic ensemble hundreds of micrometers long in free space.
main_result: The main result is an efficient compact biphoton source based on a single atom coupled to chiral waveguide modes.
application_angle: Such a source could serve scalable integrated quantum photonics and quantum-communication systems needing robust photon-pair generation.

title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can significantly distort the waveform. Here we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 km of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multi-soliton states by converting inter-soliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling sub-picosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a fundamentally new metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.
one_liner: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is used to characterize femtosecond dissipative Kerr solitons without amplification or dispersion compensation.
why_it_matters: It offers a distortion-resistant diagnostic for chip-scale microcombs, including after long fiber propagation and for multi-soliton states.
detailed_summary: The experiment attenuates dissipative Kerr soliton streams to the single-photon level and measures fourth-order Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. The interferograms recover near-transform-limited pulse durations without optical amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate after 25 km of standard fiber. Additional dips encode temporal separations in multi-soliton states, enabling sub-picosecond access to intracavity structure.
main_result: The demonstrated capability is quantum-interference metrology of microcomb soliton pulse width and multi-soliton timing without conventional ultrafast diagnostics.
application_angle: It provides a practical characterization tool for integrated frequency combs used in telecom, spectroscopy, and precision photonics.

title: Scalar Spin Chirality from Dissipative Pumping and Lamb Shift Precession
abstract: Circulating currents in triangular triple quantum dots reverse repeatedly with bias even at zero magnetic flux and for a real Hamiltonian, a phenomenon whose origin has remained unclear. We show that dissipative tunneling prepares an orbital pseudospin, while virtual charge fluctuations generate a noncollinear Lamb field that rotates it toward the chiral direction. Bias changes their relative orientation and thereby reverses the current. This reservoir-induced orbital Hanle effect converts a nonchiral orbital polarization into scalar spin chirality, which an exact ground-multiplet identity links to the circulating current. Hierarchical-equations-of-motion calculations show that the low-bias reversal survives beyond the second-order weak-coupling description, while the quadratic growth of chirality after a sudden voltage switch identifies precession. More broadly, time-reversal-odd responses can emerge in open quantum systems from the interplay between dissipative state preparation and coherent precession.
one_liner: Reservoir-driven pseudospin pumping plus Lamb-shift precession explains bias-reversible circulating currents in triangular quantum dots.
why_it_matters: The work identifies how time-reversal-odd chiral responses can arise in open quantum devices even without magnetic flux or complex Hamiltonians.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes triangular triple quantum dots where circulating currents reverse with bias at zero magnetic flux. It attributes the effect to dissipative tunneling that prepares an orbital pseudospin and virtual charge fluctuations that generate a noncollinear Lamb field, producing precession toward a chiral direction. Hierarchical-equations-of-motion calculations support the survival of low-bias reversal beyond second-order weak coupling, while voltage-switch dynamics reveal quadratic chirality growth linked to precession.
main_result: The main result is a reservoir-induced orbital Hanle mechanism converting nonchiral orbital polarization into scalar spin chirality and bias-reversible current.
application_angle: It informs control of chiral transport and open-system responses in quantum-dot hardware and mesoscopic quantum devices.

title: Ghost infrared spectroscopy with bright twin beams
abstract: Frequency-correlated light offers a route to mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy without direct spectral detection in the MIR. Previous MIR ghost spectroscopy has mainly relied on low-gain spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) and photon-pair coincidence measurements, where the limited photon flux has restricted acquisition times to longer than one minute. Here, we demonstrate ghost infrared spectroscopy using bright twin beams generated by high-gain parametric down-conversion (PDC). High-gain PDC amplifies vacuum fluctuations, producing a different pair of frequency-correlated random spectra in each pump pulse. This pulse-resolved stochastic emission is naturally matched to time-stretch detection, which records the spectrum of the correlated near-infrared telecom signal for every pulse, while the MIR idler is measured by bucket detection. Consequently, each pump pulse yields one paired projection measurement comprising a spectrally resolved reference and the corresponding bucket value. We reconstruct the transmission spectrum of a structured optical filter and the molecular vibrational absorption spectrum of liquid benzene near 3.3 um with millisecond-scale acquisition, in good agreement with Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. This reduces the acquisition time by four to five orders of magnitude compared with previous MIR ghost spectroscopy demonstrations. These results transform ghost spectroscopy from coincidence-based photon counting to high-flux analog correlation spectroscopy, establishing a practical architecture for high-speed computational infrared spectroscopy driven by a narrowband semiconductor laser.
one_liner: Bright twin beams enable millisecond mid-infrared ghost spectroscopy using telecom spectral readout and MIR bucket detection.
why_it_matters: Moving from photon-counting coincidences to high-flux analog correlations makes ghost infrared spectroscopy practically fast for chemical sensing.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses high-gain parametric down-conversion to generate pulse-resolved, frequency-correlated bright twin beams. A near-infrared telecom signal spectrum is recorded for every pulse by time-stretch detection, while the mid-infrared idler is measured with bucket detection, giving paired projection measurements. The method reconstructs a structured filter and benzene vibrational absorption near 3.3 um in milliseconds, agreeing with FTIR and improving acquisition time by four to five orders of magnitude over prior MIR ghost spectroscopy.
main_result: The demonstrated capability is millisecond-scale MIR ghost spectroscopy with analog correlations rather than coincidence photon counting.
application_angle: It enables high-speed computational infrared spectroscopy with indirect MIR spectral detection and narrowband semiconductor-laser driving.

title: Quantum non-local games: Quantum relations, projection lattices and rule operators
abstract: Quantum non-local games with quantum inputs or outputs have been formulated in several different languages, including rank-one and quantum XOR games, support maps between projection lattices, probabilistic quantum hypergraphs, and Frobenius-algebraic rule operators on finite quantum sets. We give a unified operator-algebraic comparison of these models by assigning to each rule its winning transformation space: the operator space of transformations accepted with certainty. We introduce \(\mathcal R\)-projection-test quantum games with finite-dimensional input and output von Neumann algebras and an arbitrary, possibly infinite-dimensional, referee von Neumann algebra \(\mathcal R\). Their winning transformation spaces are precisely operator spaces with a natural bimodule structure, equivalently rectangular quantum relations. We compare this formalism with projection-lattice games, hypergraph quantum games, and the graphical rule-operator definition. Projection-lattice games capture exactly the reflexive winning bimodules. Hypergraph quantum games admit value-preserving projection-test realisations, and, after passing to perfect transformations, describe the same reflexive part as projection-lattice games. Using Daws' technique, we also translate rule operators to projections in tensor products of finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras. This identification places graphical rules in the same operator-bimodule framework and preserves both values and perfectness. Finally, we compare concurrency with the synchronicity conditions of Goldberg and of Bochniak--Kasprzak--Sołtan. The framework is illustrated by classical, rank-one, quantum XOR, colouring, and quantum graph homomorphism and isomorphism games.
one_liner: Unifies several quantum non-local game formalisms through operator-space winning transformation spaces.
why_it_matters: It clarifies equivalences between game models used to reason about quantum correlations, perfect strategies, and operator-algebraic structure.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces R-projection-test quantum games with finite-dimensional input/output von Neumann algebras and a possibly infinite-dimensional referee algebra. It shows that their perfect winning transformations are exactly rectangular quantum relations with a natural bimodule structure. It also connects projection-lattice games, hypergraph games, and graphical rule operators within one operator-bimodule framework while preserving values and perfectness.
main_result: The work proves that multiple quantum non-local game definitions can be represented by the same winning-transformation operator-space formalism.
application_angle: The practical value is mainly foundational, improving formal tools for certifying quantum correlations and strategy equivalences rather than providing a hardware platform.

title: Mass-gap functional determinant approach for mobile Fermi polarons
abstract: We extend the functional determinant approach (FDA), previously restricted to static impurities, to the case of finite-mass impurities by using the mass-gap description of Fermi polarons [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 193401 (2025)]. The quadratic structure of the mass-gap model enables the exact evaluation of many-body spectra and Ramsey dynamics for mobile impurities. We show that this mass-gap FDA smoothly interpolates between the Fermi-edge singularity for infinitely heavy impurities and the emergence of quasiparticle weight for finite impurity mass. Our results demonstrate that the mass-gap FDA provides a transparent and computationally efficient framework to describe the quantum dynamics of mobile impurities.
one_liner: Extends the functional determinant approach to Ramsey dynamics of finite-mass Fermi polarons.
why_it_matters: Efficient modeling of mobile impurities supports cold-atom quantum sensing and spectroscopy where impurity motion cannot be ignored.
detailed_summary: The authors use the mass-gap description of Fermi polarons to make the functional determinant approach applicable beyond static impurities. The resulting quadratic model allows exact evaluation of many-body spectra and Ramsey response for finite-mass impurities. The method interpolates between the infinite-mass Fermi-edge singularity and finite-mass quasiparticle-weight behavior.
main_result: The paper demonstrates a computationally efficient exact framework for spectra and Ramsey dynamics of finite-mass Fermi polarons.
application_angle: It is relevant to cold-atom impurity probes, many-body Ramsey spectroscopy, and sensing protocols based on controlled impurity dynamics.

title: Gate-Efficient Implementation of the Query-Optimal Time-Dependent Hamiltonian Simulation
abstract: The query-optimal algorithm of [CGWZ26] for general time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation uses $$ q = O\left( αT + \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\left(e + \log(1/\varepsilon)/(αT) \right)} \right) $$ queries to $\mathrm{HAM\mbox{-}T}$ within $\varepsilon$ error for a Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t)$ on $[0,T]$ satisfying $\left\lVert H(t)\right\rVert\leqα$. However, its direct circuit implementation incurs a substantially larger gate overhead. In this note, we give an implementation of the same algorithm that retains its optimal query complexity and uses $$ O\left[ q \left( a + \log\left(1 + \frac{T(α+ βT)}{\varepsilon} \right) \right) \right] $$ one- and two-qubit gates, where $a$ is the number of block-encoding ancilla qubits and $β$ is the Lipschitz constant of $H$. The main ingredient is an exact dyadic factorization of the ordered update product in the underlying one-query transducer.
one_liner: Reduces gate overhead for query-optimal simulation of Lipschitz time-dependent Hamiltonians.
why_it_matters: Keeping optimal query complexity while lowering circuit cost makes time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation more realistic for fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: The note implements the CGWZ26 query-optimal time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation algorithm with substantially improved one- and two-qubit gate scaling. It preserves the optimal number of HAM-T queries while adding gate cost proportional to the query count times ancilla and logarithmic precision terms. The key construction is an exact dyadic factorization of the ordered update product in the one-query transducer.
main_result: The implementation achieves query-optimal simulation with gate complexity O[q(a + log(1 + T(alpha + beta T)/epsilon))].
application_angle: Lower gate overhead directly improves resource estimates for simulating driven molecules, materials, and control-dependent quantum systems.

title: Deterministic Universal Logical Gates for Finite-Energy GKP Qubits in Trapped Neutral Atoms
abstract: We present a universal logical gate set for finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) qubits encoded in the harmonic motional states of trapped neutral atoms. Internal electronic states serve as ancilla for implementing state-dependent conditional displacements in phase space, enabling arbitrary single-qubit phase gates. A Transient Rydberg excitation-mediated atomic dipole-dipole interaction enables a controlled-Z gate without invoking the blockade mechanism. The gates operate under magic-trapping conditions, allowing continuous trapping throughout the gate sequence, thereby preserving the motional encoding without intermediate measurement or feedforward. We assess the experimental feasibility of the proposed protocols using neutral $^{88}\mathrm{Sr}$ atoms and obtain average gate fidelities of $0.986$ for single-qubit phase gates and $0.985$ for the controlled-Z gate at a finite squeezing parameter of $Δ=0.25$ (12 dB of squeezing), increasing to $0.997$ and $0.995$ respectively as $Δ$ reaches $0.1$. These results provide a route toward universal, measurement-free logical control of motional GKP qubits in neutral-atom architectures.
one_liner: Proposes deterministic universal gates for finite-energy motional GKP qubits in trapped neutral atoms.
why_it_matters: It offers a measurement-free route to logical GKP control compatible with continuous trapping in a scalable neutral-atom architecture.
detailed_summary: The paper encodes finite-energy GKP qubits in harmonic motional states of trapped neutral Sr-88 atoms and uses internal electronic states as ancillas for conditional phase-space displacements. Single-qubit phase gates and a controlled-Z gate are implemented deterministically, with the two-qubit gate mediated by transient Rydberg dipole-dipole interaction rather than blockade. Under magic-trapping conditions, the proposed gates maintain confinement and avoid intermediate measurement or feedforward.
main_result: The authors estimate average fidelities near 0.986 for single-qubit phase gates and 0.985 for CZ at 12 dB squeezing, improving at stronger squeezing.
application_angle: The scheme targets practical logical control for bosonic-error-corrected neutral-atom processors without measurement-based gate overhead.

title: Coexistence of polariton bound states in the continuum and 2D radiative excitons
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) enable optical modes with ideally infinite radiative lifetimes despite lying within the radiation continuum. Radiation-matter interaction in periodically patterned planar waveguides embedding two-dimensional (2D) optically active excitations can be described quantum mechanically by diagonalizing a non-Hermitian operator, known as the Hopfield matrix, which can be generalized to incorporate independent photonic and excitonic losses into the polaritonic states. However, since 2D excitons undergo intrinsic wavevector-dependent radiative decay within the light cone, whether the Hopfield formalism can consistently account for this process while preserving polariton BICs has remained an open question. Here we show that a non-Hermitian Hopfield formalism incorporating excitonic radiative losses correctly captures the existence of genuine $k=0$ polariton BICs with diverging radiative lifetimes. The theory provides a unified microscopic framework for radiative excitons and polariton BICs, and an efficient predictive tool for designing photonic-crystal platforms coupled to quantum wells, transition-metal dichalcogenides, and other 2D excitonic materials.
one_liner: Shows polariton BICs can coexist consistently with radiatively decaying 2D excitons.
why_it_matters: A unified non-Hermitian Hopfield model gives designers a tool for high-Q polaritonic devices using quantum wells or 2D materials.
detailed_summary: The work extends the non-Hermitian Hopfield formalism to include intrinsic wavevector-dependent radiative decay of 2D excitons inside the light cone. It shows that this treatment still supports genuine k=0 polariton bound states in the continuum with diverging radiative lifetime. The framework combines photonic and excitonic loss channels in a microscopic design model for patterned planar waveguides.
main_result: The paper demonstrates theoretically that excitonic radiative loss can be included while preserving true polariton BICs at k=0.
application_angle: This supports design of high-Q polaritonic components, low-threshold emitters, and exciton-photon platforms based on quantum wells or TMD monolayers.

title: Quantum Block Turbo Codes
authors: Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
abstract: In the early nineties, the introduction of turbo codes revolutionized classical error correction. The idea was mainly applied on two types of codes: convolutional turbo codes and turbo product codes. The first type of codes was adapted to quantum error correction which initiated the theory of quantum serial turbo codes. In this paper, we present a theory for quantum block turbo codes, the quantum analog of the second type of turbo codes. We describe their iterative decoding algorithm and simulate their performances on a depolarizing channel for different constituent codes.
one_liner: Introduces quantum block turbo codes and iterative decoding for depolarizing-noise channels.
why_it_matters: Turbo-style block-code concatenation could expand practical quantum error-correction options for noisy quantum processors and links.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a quantum analogue of classical turbo product codes, complementing prior quantum serial turbo-code work. It defines quantum block turbo codes, presents an iterative decoding algorithm, and simulates performance for several constituent codes under depolarizing noise. The emphasis is on code construction and decoder behavior rather than a specific hardware implementation.
main_result: The authors formulate quantum block turbo codes and evaluate iterative decoding performance on depolarizing channels.
application_angle: Improved code families and decoders are relevant to fault-tolerant computing stacks and quantum communication channels that need efficient error correction.

title: Neutral atom quantum computing
abstract: Neutral atom qubits are one of the leading approaches for implementation of a large scale quantum computer. The original proposals for neutral atom qubits were formulated more than 25 years ago, with first demonstrations of a universal gate set following 10 years later. In the last few years the performance and scale of neutral atom qubit arrays has developed at a rapid pace leading to demonstrations of quantum algorithms, and logical qubits for fault tolerant error correction. This contribution reviews the physics of the neutral atom approach, surveys current capabilities, and provides an outlook for future progress.
one_liner: A review of neutral-atom quantum computing physics, current array capabilities, and paths toward scalable fault-tolerant machines.
why_it_matters: Neutral atoms are now a leading hardware route because large reconfigurable arrays, improved gates, algorithms, and logical-qubit demonstrations are converging.
detailed_summary: The paper reviews the neutral-atom approach to quantum computing, from trapping and control physics to universal gate implementations. It surveys recent progress in scaling atom arrays, executing quantum algorithms, and demonstrating logical qubits for error correction. The outlook frames remaining challenges for reliable gates, connectivity, control overhead, and fault-tolerant scaling.
main_result: The work synthesizes the state of neutral-atom quantum computing and identifies current capabilities supporting large-scale fault-tolerant development.
application_angle: It is directly relevant to quantum-processor roadmapping, hardware benchmarking, and architecture choices for scalable quantum computers.

title: Photon-efficient quantum repeater chains via hyperentanglement-assisted purification
abstract: Linear quantum repeater chains based on Werner-state purification (the BBPSSW protocol) and entanglement swapping (the BDCZ scheme) are fundamental to entanglement distribution in quantum networks. However, they operate under a stringent operation reliability threshold and rely on resource-intensive recurrence purification rounds, each consuming two entangled pairs to probabilistically produce one. In the literature, hyperentanglement has been proposed to exploit multiple degrees of freedom (DOF), such as polarisation and spatial modes, to encode independent entangled states within a single photon pair. This has led to the definition of DAEPP (DOF-Assisted Entanglement Purification Protocol), which we propose to integrate with the BDCZ scheme, resulting in a chain protocol that we call DAHR (DOF-Assisted Hyperentanglement Repeater). The DAEPP step distils the fidelity of a DOF by consuming other(s). In this work, we propose and analyse a DAHR variant which integrates DAEPP at every segment of an end-to-end path combined with BDCZ. We derive a closed-form end-to-end fidelity recursion that embeds single-segment DAEPP into the BDCZ scheme and give a strict resource lower bound for any BDCZ baseline utilising BBPSSW purification to match DAHR's per-segment effective fidelity. At a representative asymmetric operating point informed by prior experiment, we show numerically that matching DAHR's single-photon-pair performance requires two to three rounds of BBPSSW purification. Additionally, below a critical operation reliability, no amount of BBPSSW rounds matches DAHR's one DAEPP round performance.
one_liner: Hyperentanglement-assisted purification is integrated into repeater chains to improve photon efficiency over BBPSSW-based baselines.
why_it_matters: The protocol can reduce entangled-pair consumption and relax operation-reliability constraints for long-distance entanglement distribution.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes DAHR, a degree-of-freedom-assisted hyperentanglement repeater protocol combining DAEPP purification with BDCZ entanglement swapping. It derives a closed-form end-to-end fidelity recursion and a strict lower bound on BBPSSW resources needed to match the DAHR effective segment fidelity. Numerical examples show that two to three BBPSSW rounds may be required to match one DAHR operation, and below a critical reliability no BBPSSW recurrence depth catches up.
main_result: The main result is a repeater-chain formulation where one hyperentangled photon pair can outperform resource-intensive recurrence purification at representative operating points.
application_angle: This targets more photon-efficient quantum-network links and could inform architectures for scalable entanglement distribution.

title: Towards Site-Selective Fabrication of Near-Infrared Emitters in hBN
abstract: Spatial control of near-infrared (NIR) emission from hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) would facilitate coupling atomic-scale light sources to photonic structures, yet oxygen-related NIR emitters are generally formed at stochastic locations. Here, we combine single-shot femtosecond laser writing with annealing in an oxygen-rich environment to bias NIR activation toward predefined coordinates in exfoliated hBN. Spectra acquired with 532, 635, and 785 nm excitations show narrow and multipeak emission extending to a wavelength of 1 um. Among the spectra collected at written sites, over 83% under 785 nm excitation and 71% under 635 nm excitation contain at least one resolved peak above 810 nm. The emission intensity increases monotonically with writing-pulse energy, suggesting tunability and indicating that the optimum for the single-emitter regime may require lower energies. Band-pass-resolved measurements show zero-delay correlation dips with g2(0) values indicative of single-photon emission but also reveal contributions from the spectral background. Spectrally resolved time series under 785 nm excitation show persistent bands over the recorded intervals as well as intermittent emission above 900 nm. This approach demonstrates NIR-emitter activation at predefined sites while identifying residual off-site activation and spectral multiplicity as the principal targets for further optimization.
one_liner: Femtosecond laser writing plus oxygen annealing biases near-infrared hBN emitter activation toward predefined sites.
why_it_matters: Position-controlled NIR emitters in hBN would make it easier to integrate atomic-scale photon sources with nanophotonic devices.
detailed_summary: The study uses single-shot femtosecond laser writing followed by oxygen-rich annealing to activate NIR emission at selected coordinates in exfoliated hBN. Spectroscopy under 532, 635, and 785 nm excitation shows resolved emission peaks extending to about 1 um, with high yield above 810 nm at written sites. Correlation measurements show antibunching signatures but also reveal spectral background, while time traces show persistent and intermittent NIR bands.
main_result: The work demonstrates biased activation of NIR-emitting hBN defects at predefined sites with measurable single-photon-emission signatures.
application_angle: Site selectivity is important for coupling hBN emitters to cavities, waveguides, and integrated quantum-photonic circuits.

title: Size-Independent Robustness in Multipartite Bell Self-Testing
abstract: Practical robust self-testing of multipartite entanglement has so far been restricted to small-scale systems due to error bounds that degrade severely with system size. In this work, we establish multipartite self-testing with robustness independent of the size of the quantum network. We derive a fully analytic, device-independent self-testing bound for $n$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states. The bound scales linearly with the observed violation error and lies universally within a constant factor of two from a theoretical upper bound. Furthermore, the operator-inequality framework reduces the verification of the conjectured optimal bound to a highly efficient numerical check, which we perform up to $n=100$. Consequently, GHZ entanglement can be certified under a fixed noise level in arbitrarily large systems, enabling scalable device-independent verification.
one_liner: An analytic device-independent GHZ self-testing bound is derived with robustness independent of network size.
why_it_matters: Scalable certification of multipartite entanglement is essential for large quantum networks and distributed quantum protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a fully analytic device-independent self-testing bound for n-qubit GHZ states. Its robustness scales linearly with observed violation error and does not degrade with the number of parties, remaining within a constant factor of a theoretical upper bound. The operator-inequality framework also reduces the conjectured optimal-bound check to efficient numerics, demonstrated up to n=100.
main_result: The main result is size-independent robust self-testing for GHZ entanglement under fixed noise levels.
application_angle: This improves practical verification tools for large distributed quantum systems without trusting internal device models.

title: Signatures of inter-sideband coherence in the resonance fluorescence spectrum of an acoustically-modulated quantum dot
abstract: We theoretically investigate the inter-sideband phase coherence within the resonance fluorescence spectrum of an acoustically modulated quantum dot using a filtered-field formalism for a Mach-Zehnder configuration. We demonstrate that geometric slant of the interferograms provides an indicator of phase coherence that is resilient to environmental white noise. Specifically, noise-induced spectral diffusion reduces the global fringe intensity, while leaving the characteristic inclination strictly invariant. Our findings establish a framework for verifying single-photon coherence between spectral sidebands, essential for frequency-bin encoding and scalable quantum networking in realistic, noisy solid-state architectures.
one_liner: A filtered-field Mach-Zehnder analysis predicts noise-resilient interferogram signatures of quantum-dot sideband coherence.
why_it_matters: Verifying sideband coherence is a key step toward frequency-bin photonic encoding with solid-state single-photon sources.
detailed_summary: The paper theoretically studies resonance fluorescence from an acoustically modulated quantum dot using a filtered-field formalism for a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. It shows that the geometric slant of interferograms serves as a phase-coherence indicator between spectral sidebands. White-noise spectral diffusion reduces overall fringe contrast but leaves the slant invariant, making the signature robust in noisy solid-state settings.
main_result: The work identifies interferogram inclination as a robust observable for inter-sideband single-photon coherence.
application_angle: The result supports frequency-bin encoding and quantum-network interfaces based on practical solid-state photon sources.

title: Quantum Dot Colloidosomes as Triggerable Microlasers
abstract: Quantum dot (QD) supraparticle lasers are promising platforms for microscale light sources and photonic labeling, yet their optical properties are set during assembly. Here we introduce QD colloidosomes, liquid-core/solid-shell supraparticles that combine whispering-gallery-mode optical feedback with stimulus-triggered structural collapse. Intact QD colloidosomes show cavity-defined lasing with fluence thresholds of ~2.8 mJ/cm2 and linewidths of 2.2-3.7 nm, demonstrating efficient light trapping without a solid core. We identify shell continuity as a critical determinant for whispering-gallery feedback and lasing by exploring a morphological continuum of suprastructures comprising solid supraparticles, colloidosomes, and microporous hollow shells. Intact colloidosomes support narrow cavity modes, whereas porous shells remain broadband even at high pump fluence. We show that colloidosomes can be driven to rupture and release payload through well-defined pathways, including meniscus-driven capillary failure, uniform heating, and localized near-infrared activation, thereby reconfiguring their optical response from cavity-defined lasing to broadband emission. These results establish QD colloidosomes as reconfigurable microlasers that couple optical-state switching and triggered release within a single self-assembled platform.
one_liner: Liquid-core quantum-dot colloidosomes act as triggerable whispering-gallery microlasers with switchable optical response.
why_it_matters: Reconfigurable microlasers that combine optical signaling and triggered payload release could benefit photonic labels and microscale devices.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces QD colloidosomes with liquid cores and solid shells that provide whispering-gallery-mode feedback. Intact structures lase with thresholds around 2.8 mJ/cm2 and linewidths of 2.2-3.7 nm, while porous shells remain broadband, highlighting shell continuity as crucial. Mechanical, thermal, and localized NIR triggering can rupture the structures and switch emission from cavity-defined lasing to broadband output.
main_result: The main result is a self-assembled QD microlaser platform whose lasing state can be switched through controlled structural collapse.
application_angle: The platform is relevant for stimulus-responsive photonic labeling, microscale light sources, and release-coupled optical sensing.

title: Terrestrial Gravitational Wave Detection with Atom Interferometers
abstract: Atom interferometers (AIFs) are highly precise inertial sensors and are considered promising instruments for the detection of gravitational waves (GWs) and certain dark matter (DM) candidates in the mid-frequency band. While GW detection with AIFs was initially proposed for space-based experiments with baselines spanning thousands of kilometers, recent developments suggest that terrestrial setups with baselines of at least 100 meters may also be capable of detecting GWs. In this work, we analytically derive the GW phase response formula of a ground detector, find an additional term compared to the existing literature and check it our findings numerically. Based on this treatment, we analyze the optimal geometric parameters for earth-bound AIF experiments. Subsequently, we numerically simulate GW detection schemes for these optimized interferometers using an open-source Python algorithm. Numerical simulations of these schemes have are not available to the community, yet crucial for the accurate modeling of noise and non-trivial gravitational backgrounds.
one_liner: Analytical and numerical modeling refines terrestrial atom-interferometer responses to mid-band gravitational waves.
why_it_matters: Ground-based 100 m-scale atom interferometers could extend GW and dark-matter sensing if geometry, phase response, and backgrounds are modeled accurately.
detailed_summary: The paper derives the gravitational-wave phase response for a ground-based atom-interferometer detector and reports an additional term relative to prior treatments. It then uses the response model to optimize terrestrial detector geometry and simulate detection schemes with an open-source Python algorithm. The emphasis is on realistic modeling of noise and nontrivial gravitational backgrounds for at least 100 m baselines.
main_result: The work provides a corrected analytical phase-response model and numerical simulation workflow for optimized ground-based AIF gravitational-wave detection.
application_angle: It supports design studies for practical terrestrial mid-frequency GW and dark-matter detectors using atom interferometry.

title: Protected Logical Qudits in Kitaev Quantum Double Models via Stable Representations
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires robust protection of encoded quantum information. In this work, we develop a representation-theoretic framework for constructing protected logical qudits in finite-group Kitaev quantum double models. By introducing $\varepsilon$-stable irreducible representations, we establish a necessary and sufficient existence criterion and derive ribbon--projector commutation relations that yield a $d$-dimensional protected logical subspace. We apply this construction to symmetric and alternating groups, obtaining logical qubits for $S_n$ ($n\ge 3$) and a logical qutrit for $A_4$. Moreover, the family $(\mathbb Z_2)^d\rtimes\mathbb Z_d$ realizes protected logical qudits of arbitrary dimension $d\ge 2$. Finally, for $D(A_4)$, we describe a scheme for universal logical qutrit computation using ribbon-based logical operations.
one_liner: Representation theory is used to build protected logical qudits in finite-group Kitaev quantum double codes.
why_it_matters: It expands the design space for topological quantum hardware by giving criteria and examples for protected qubit, qutrit, and arbitrary-qudit encodings.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce epsilon-stable irreducible representations as a criterion for protected logical subspaces in finite-group Kitaev quantum double models. They derive ribbon-projector commutation relations yielding d-dimensional logical qudit spaces, with examples in symmetric and alternating groups. They also outline universal logical qutrit computation for D(A4) using ribbon-based operations.
main_result: The paper gives necessary and sufficient representation-theoretic conditions for protected logical qudits and constructs explicit qubit, qutrit, and arbitrary-dimension examples.
application_angle: The framework can guide topological code and logical-gate design for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

title: Phase-noise induced many-body interference suppression in Gaussian Boson Sampling
abstract: We develop a Heisenberg-picture tensor-network formulation of collision-free Gaussian Boson Sampling, providing a direct Fock-space expression for output probabilities in terms of experimentally accessible quantities. The resulting representation naturally recovers the Hafnian structure while revealing the decomposition of GBS probability into a phase-insensitive contribution and a hierarchy of interference sectors associated with pairs of perfect matchings. As an application, we investigate phase diffusion and show how it progressively suppresses many-body interference, driving the output statistics toward a classical dimer-model regime. Our results establish a transparent framework for connecting experimentally characterized phase fluctuations with the loss of quantum interference in photonic quantum sampling experiments.
one_liner: A tensor-network GBS formulation links measured phase noise to suppression of many-body photonic interference.
why_it_matters: It gives experimentalists a route to quantify how phase diffusion degrades quantum advantage in Gaussian Boson Sampling devices.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a Heisenberg-picture tensor-network formulation for collision-free Gaussian Boson Sampling output probabilities in Fock space. The representation recovers Hafnian structure while decomposing probabilities into phase-insensitive and interference-sector contributions. Applying the formalism to phase diffusion shows a progressive transition toward classical dimer-model statistics as many-body interference is suppressed.
main_result: The main result is a calculable framework connecting experimentally characterized phase fluctuations to loss of many-body interference in GBS outputs.
application_angle: It helps benchmark and diagnose photonic quantum sampling hardware under realistic phase-noise conditions.

title: Device characterization of Si$/$SiGe double quantum dots using exchange oscillations in Earth's magnetic field
abstract: Exchange-based semiconductor qubits encompass a broad family of encodings constructed from singlet- and triplet-like spin states, several of which are compatible with operation at zero applied magnetic field. Their reliable operation requires characterization of environmental noise, residual idle interactions, and exchange-dependent decay, but this characterization often relies on multi-axis control calibration or deliberately engineered magnetic-field gradients. A simpler zero-applied-field diagnostic is particularly valuable for hybrid semiconductor-superconductor systems, in which magnetic fields can degrade superconducting components. Here, we use the intrinsic magnetic-field gradient produced by residual nuclear spins in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe to implement exchange oscillations between two quantum dots as a characterization tool without a micromagnet, dynamic nuclear polarization, or prior multi-axis calibration. Using Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill exchange sequences, we extend the singlet coherence from $T_2^*=1.17\pm0.02~μ$s to $T_2^{\mathrm{CPMG}}=74.8\pm1.8~μ$s with $N=70$ refocusing pulses. The oscillation phase resolves residual exchange in the tens-of-kilohertz regime and enables it to be mapped across the $(1,1)$ charge cell. These results establish intrinsic-gradient exchange oscillations as a simple, more relevant zero-field diagnostic for exchange-only and related semiconductor qubit encodings that is amenable to rapid, high-throughput device characterization.
one_liner: Intrinsic nuclear-spin gradients enable zero-applied-field exchange-oscillation diagnostics in Si/SiGe double dots.
why_it_matters: The method avoids micromagnets and applied fields, making fast semiconductor-qubit characterization more compatible with superconducting hybrids.
detailed_summary: The study uses residual nuclear-spin magnetic-field gradients in isotopically enriched Si/SiGe to drive exchange oscillations between singlet- and triplet-like states without micromagnets or dynamic nuclear polarization. CPMG exchange sequences extend singlet coherence from T2*=1.17 us to T2^CPMG=74.8 us with 70 refocusing pulses. The oscillation phase resolves residual exchange at tens-of-kilohertz levels and maps it across the (1,1) charge cell.
main_result: The authors demonstrate zero-applied-field exchange-oscillation characterization and residual-exchange mapping using intrinsic gradients.
application_angle: This is a practical diagnostic for high-throughput tuning of exchange-only semiconductor qubits and hybrid superconducting-semiconductor devices.

title: Tunable Exceptional Points for Quantum Sensing in a Spin--Orbit-Angular-Momentum Coupled BEC
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) can induce strongly amplified responses to weak perturbations, but enhanced spectral sensitivity in conventional non-Hermitian systems does not necessarily translate into improved quantum-limited sensing because of the associated gain and loss noise. Here, we investigate a tunable EP sensing platform based on the intrinsic non-Hermitian Bogoliubov dynamics of a spin-orbit-angular-momentum-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. Starting from a fully Hermitian microscopic Hamiltonian, we derive a Bogoliubov dynamical matrix that exhibits parity-time (PT) symmetry, with EPs tunable through the Raman coupling and interaction parameters. We identify multiple EPs and map their trajectories and associated stability landscapes, revealing strong quantum Fisher information enhancement when the EPs are approached from the PT-symmetric stable regime. We further find that the gap-opening rate around a second-order EP provides a useful relative indicator for comparing the sensing performance of EPs, while higher-order EPs are not necessarily accessible from the stable regime. Moreover, two second-order EPs can be tuned to overlap, allowing their sensing contributions to add and yielding a linear enhancement of the total quantum Fisher information. Finally, we show that a spin-density measurement can approach the quantum Fisher information limit, providing an experimentally accessible route to tunable EP-enhanced quantum sensing in Bose-Einstein condensates.
one_liner: Tunable exceptional points in a spin-orbit-angular-momentum BEC enhance quantum Fisher information for sensing.
why_it_matters: It identifies a stable-regime route to EP-enhanced sensing without relying on noisy external gain-loss engineering.
detailed_summary: The paper derives a non-Hermitian Bogoliubov dynamical matrix from a Hermitian microscopic Hamiltonian for a spin-orbit-angular-momentum-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. It maps tunable exceptional points controlled by Raman coupling and interactions, emphasizing access from the PT-symmetric stable regime. Near suitable second-order EPs, quantum Fisher information is enhanced, and spin-density measurements can approach the quantum limit.
main_result: The work shows that tunable stable-regime exceptional points can enhance QFI and that overlapping second-order EPs can add sensing contributions linearly.
application_angle: It proposes an experimentally accessible BEC platform for tunable EP-enhanced quantum sensing.

title: Engineering multi-photon dissipation with a dc-voltage-biased Josephson junction
abstract: Multi-photon dissipation -- a key resource for bosonic qubits -- is usually realized by parametrically pumping a Josephson coupler at the cost of spurious nonlinear terms. Here we instead engineer it using a dc-voltage-biased SQUID, such that these parasitic terms average out. We activate the conversion of one, two, or four photons of a high-Q mode into a single photon of a lossy mode. We characterize the two-photon dissipation by Wigner tomography, establishing dc-biased junctions as a resource for reservoir engineering and a viable route to cat-qubit stabilization.
one_liner: A dc-voltage-biased SQUID engineers one-, two-, and four-photon dissipation for bosonic modes.
why_it_matters: Cleaner multi-photon loss channels are central to reservoir engineering and hardware-efficient cat-qubit stabilization.
detailed_summary: The authors use a dc-voltage-biased SQUID to convert one, two, or four photons from a high-Q mode into a single photon of a lossy mode. Unlike parametric pumping of Josephson couplers, the dc-biased approach is designed so parasitic nonlinear terms average out. Two-photon dissipation is characterized by Wigner tomography, supporting its use for engineered reservoirs.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates selectable multi-photon dissipation channels, including Wigner-tomography characterization of two-photon dissipation.
application_angle: It offers a circuit-QED route toward stabilized cat qubits and bosonic error-protection hardware.

title: Efficient search for excitable zero-modes in constrained systems
abstract: Kinetically constrained systems, such as those representing Rydberg atom arrays in the blockade regime, have gathered considerable attention due to the presence of atypical eigenstates in their spectrum. The latter manifests itself through the presence of quantum many-body scars as well as unusually large zero-mode (ZM) subspaces which contain analytically tractable eigenstates with various entanglement scalings. In particular, some of the latter are excitable zero-modes (EZMs), meaning that they can be promoted to a non-zero energy for open boundary conditions. In this work, I present an efficient protocol for finding analytical expressions for translation-invariant EZMs in constrained systems, based on the eigendecomposition of the local unconstrained Hamiltonian. I demonstrate the power of this method on a decorated Rydberg chain. In that model, my protocol directly produces a continuous matrix-product-state manifold located entirely in the zero-energy eigenspace for periodic boundary conditions. The span of that manifold grows exponentially with the system, and for odd system sizes it covers the entire zero-momentum eigenspace with zero energy. I then show how the physical structure of the manifold, which is tied to the local eigenbasis, also allows one to derive analytical expressions for ZMs at non-zero momentum and for a polynomial number of exact scars at $E=\pm\sqrt{3}$.
one_liner: Efficient construction of exact zero-modes and scars in constrained Rydberg-like chains via local Hamiltonian eigendecomposition.
why_it_matters: Gives analytic structure for scarred constrained dynamics relevant to programmable Rydberg-array quantum simulators and hardware benchmarking.
detailed_summary: The paper presents a protocol for finding translation-invariant excitable zero-modes in kinetically constrained systems by diagonalizing the local unconstrained Hamiltonian. Applied to a decorated Rydberg chain, it yields a continuous matrix-product-state manifold entirely within the periodic-boundary zero-energy subspace, with exponentially growing span. The same local-eigenbasis structure is used to derive nonzero-momentum zero-modes and exact scar states at finite energies.
main_result: The method analytically generates extensive zero-mode manifolds and polynomially many exact scar states in a constrained Rydberg-chain model.
application_angle: Provides tractable target states and diagnostics for quantum simulation experiments using Rydberg atom arrays.

title: Searching for Axions on a Higher Note: Third-Harmonic Generation from Colliding High-Intensity Laser Beams
abstract: We propose a new laboratory strategy to generate and detect axion-like particles via third-harmonic generation induced by two non-collinear, polarised high-intensity laser beams of peak intensity of the order of $10^{24}\,\mathrm{W/cm^2}$, where the third-harmonic signal is generated by the axion field. Starting from the axion-modified Maxwell equations, we analytically derive the axion-induced third-harmonic field, and show that by using state-of-the-art petawatt laser facilities, a detectable signal can be obtained over a broad range of axion masses and couplings. A key feature of the setup is that the axion-photon conversion rate can be resonantly enhanced by tuning the angle between the two beams through a mechanism that does not depend on the physical volume of the apparatus. The proposed configuration may therefore probe an unexplored region of axion parameter space and pave the way for next-generation high-power laser-based axion searches.
one_liner: Proposes resonantly enhanced axion searches using axion-induced third-harmonic generation from colliding petawatt laser beams.
why_it_matters: Turns high-intensity nonlinear photonics into a tabletop probe of axion-like particles with angle-tunable resonance and no volume-scaling penalty.
detailed_summary: The work derives an axion-induced third-harmonic field from axion-modified Maxwell equations for two non-collinear polarized laser beams. It predicts detectable signals at peak intensities near 10^24 W/cm^2 using state-of-the-art petawatt facilities. The conversion can be resonantly enhanced by tuning the beam-crossing angle, enabling sensitivity over broad axion mass and coupling ranges.
main_result: The proposed optical geometry can generate a detectable axion-mediated third-harmonic signal with angle-tunable resonant enhancement.
application_angle: Offers a laser-based route to explore axion parameter space without relying on large-volume detector apparatus.

title: Encoding Compact U(1) Gauge Fields in Bosonic Modes with GKP Stabilization
abstract: Compact lattice gauge theories are formulated in terms of angular variables and integer electric fluxes, while bosonic quantum hardware provides oscillator modes with continuous, unbounded quadratures. We bridge this gap with a one-to-one encoding. After Gauss's law is solved, each remaining gauge degree of freedom is carried by a single oscillator mode, with its interactions built from trigonometric gates, and a Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP)-type stabilizer provides the compactness that the hardware does not. The encoding becomes exact in the limit of infinite squeezing, and at finite squeezing, the leading imperfections act as small, computable shifts of physical observables rather than uncontrolled leakage. We apply the construction to compact QED$_3$ and derive the error budget at finite squeezing, characterizing the leading errors in closed form, and showing that they can be corrected, subtracted, or extrapolated away. We construct syndrome-extraction protocols that detect and remove the displacement component of photon loss, delimit the noise it does not reach, compare two choices of dynamical variables, and collect the scaling of mode count, gate count, and measurement cost. A one-plaquette example reproduces the exact compact-rotor dynamics, and real-time spectroscopy with controlled extrapolations recovers the exponentially small energy splitting between charge sectors, the seed of the monopole physics of the theory, at the percent level against its exact value.
one_liner: Maps compact U(1) lattice gauge degrees of freedom onto oscillator modes stabilized by GKP-type compactness constraints.
why_it_matters: Connects bosonic quantum hardware to compact gauge-theory simulation with explicit finite-squeezing error budgets and correction protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper gives a one-to-one oscillator encoding for compact lattice gauge fields after solving Gauss's law, using trigonometric gates for interactions and GKP-type stabilizers to impose compactness. At finite squeezing, leading errors become calculable shifts in observables rather than uncontrolled leakage. For compact QED3, it derives closed-form error budgets, photon-loss syndrome extraction methods, resource scalings, and a one-plaquette demonstration recovering compact-rotor dynamics and charge-sector splittings.
main_result: The encoding reproduces compact-gauge dynamics in oscillator hardware with controllable finite-squeezing and photon-loss error mechanisms.
application_angle: Enables analog-digital simulation of lattice gauge physics on bosonic platforms such as microwave or optical oscillator processors.

title: Exact learning of quantum noise with tensor networks
abstract: Accurate noise models are essential for high-performance quantum error correction, yet characterizing the noise of a quantum device typically requires dedicated experiments. We present a variational framework that learns the noise model directly from quantum-error-correction syndrome and logical-observable data collected during error-corrected memory experiments. The fault-event probabilities are treated as variational parameters and optimized via gradient descent to minimize the binary cross-entropy between the decoder's predictions and experimental logical-observable outcomes. We prove that this objective is principled rather than ad hoc: a sufficiently expressive noise ansatz attains the information-theoretic minimum logical error rate. We instantiate this framework using a tensor-network decoder, which provides exact maximum-likelihood decoding and analytically differentiable gradients with respect to all noise parameters. Using circuit-level data from Google's Sycamore processor, and starting from an uninformed prior, the optimization recovers noise models whose logical error rates agree to within $2\%$ with those of Google's independently characterized detector error model. The mean squared error between the learned and reference noise parameters shows a clear overall decrease throughout training, confirming that the method recovers physically meaningful noise structure, not merely parameters that happen to decode well. We further demonstrate that the optimization can track device drifts in real time via warm-started updates, maintaining near-optimal decoding performance under synthetically evolving noise without the need for re-characterization. The approach is decoder-agnostic in its formulation and naturally extends to correlated noise models.
one_liner: Learns circuit-level quantum noise directly from QEC syndrome and logical data using differentiable tensor-network decoding.
why_it_matters: Reduces dependence on separate calibration experiments while improving practical noise tracking for error-corrected quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a variational framework where fault-event probabilities are optimized from memory-experiment syndrome and logical-observable data. A tensor-network decoder supplies exact maximum-likelihood decoding and analytic gradients for all noise parameters. On Google Sycamore circuit-level data, the learned models match independently characterized logical error rates within 2% and can be warm-started to track synthetic device drift.
main_result: The method recovers physically meaningful noise parameters from QEC data and maintains near-optimal decoding under drifting noise.
application_angle: Supports online noise learning and decoder adaptation for scalable quantum error correction workflows.

title: Modeling and Optimization of Cascaded Four-Wave Mixing toward the VUV in Xenon-Filled Negative-Curvature Fibers
abstract: In this work, we thoroughly characterize third- and fourth-harmonic generation through cascaded four-wave mixing in a xenon-filled negative-curvature hollow-core fiber operated under a pressure gradient. The experimental results are supported by both a semi-analytical model and numerical simulations, which accurately reproduce the pressure dependence of the harmonic conversion. We identify the optimum pressure conditions for third and fourth-harmonic generation and experimentally observe the cascaded four-wave-mixing process extending into the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), up to the sixth harmonic at 172 nm, with the accessible spectral range limited by the available VUV filter.
one_liner: Models and optimizes cascaded four-wave mixing to generate VUV harmonics in xenon-filled negative-curvature hollow-core fiber.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates pressure-tuned fiber nonlinear optics as a compact route to coherent VUV generation down to 172 nm.
detailed_summary: The study characterizes third- and fourth-harmonic generation through cascaded four-wave mixing in xenon-filled negative-curvature fiber under a pressure gradient. Semi-analytical modeling and numerical simulations reproduce the measured pressure dependence of harmonic conversion. The experiment identifies optimum pressures and observes cascaded generation into the VUV up to the sixth harmonic at 172 nm, limited by available filtering.
main_result: The system produces optimized third and fourth harmonics and observes cascaded VUV generation up to 172 nm.
application_angle: Provides a tunable fiber-based source concept for VUV spectroscopy, materials probing, and ultrafast photonics.

title: Spatial correlations of photons interacting via transverse Rydberg blockade
abstract: We develop a theory of the transverse spatial dynamics of two interacting photons in a Rydberg nonlinear medium. Extending the well-studied one-dimensional case, we explore both longitudinal and transverse correlations of photons propagating as Rydberg polaritons. We identify distinct behaviors and scaling laws for these correlations, arising from fundamentally different mechanisms in the two directions: diffraction for transverse correlations and diffusion for longitudinal correlations. We develop a model incorporating a Gaussian optical beam and an inhomogeneous atomic density distribution, from which we derive quantitative predictions for correlation functions in both directions. We further show that the propagation equations can be reduced to a single Schrödinger-like equation, allowing approximate solutions that are supported by full numerical results. Our findings indicate that the transverse correlation length is determined primarily by the blockade radius, whereas the longitudinal correlation length is limited by bandwidth. These results establish transverse Rydberg blockade as a distinct and measurable correlation mechanism and show that spatial photon correlations provide a direct means of measuring the blockade radius.
one_liner: Develops theory for transverse and longitudinal photon-pair correlations in Rydberg nonlinear media under transverse blockade.
why_it_matters: Identifies spatial correlation signatures that can directly measure Rydberg blockade radius and guide photon-photon gate media design.
detailed_summary: The paper extends two-photon Rydberg-polariton theory to transverse spatial dynamics, including Gaussian beam profiles and inhomogeneous atomic density. It separates transverse correlations governed by diffraction from longitudinal correlations governed by diffusion and bandwidth. A reduced Schrödinger-like equation gives approximate solutions supported by full numerics, with transverse correlation length set mainly by the blockade radius.
main_result: The theory predicts distinct transverse and longitudinal photon-correlation scalings and links transverse correlation length to the blockade radius.
application_angle: Guides experiments using spatial photon correlations to characterize Rydberg media for nonlinear quantum optics and photonic gates.

title: Towards unsupervised representation learning for quantum data: quantum models with inference and generation
abstract: With quantum sensors, simulators and networks emerging, a future of quantum technology may produce quantum states as data---that is, coherently rather than as classical measurement records---thus motivating the study of suitable quantum generalisations of modern machine learning, including the automated, unsupervised extraction of useful representations. Two ingredients are central to the latter: inference, mapping observations to latent representations, and generation, mapping latent states back to synthetic data. Both are related to each other and to joint distributions for training models by the chain-rule of classical probability theory. The fact that quantum states however lack such universal, standard factorisation property thus poses a challenge. Here we develop a conceptual and mathematical framework for unsupervised representation learning from quantum data. Models are joint quantum states over visible and latent systems; state-over-time maps provide a notion of factorisation into a marginal state and inference (generation) channel; models with inference (generation) are ambiguous states---states for which such factorisation obtains---subject to a further consistency condition on extended inference maps as data extension. These stipulations are restrictive: we show that non-trivial models must feature non-linear such maps to the extended space. For three representative state-over-time maps, we completely characterise the ambiguous states, uncovering a hierarchy tied to the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion from entanglement theory. Notably, the Leifer-Spekkens construction supports inference and generation exactly for model classes of PPT states, thus allowing genuinely quantum visible-latent correlations. We also formulate quantum counterparts of exact and approximate inference training, explore weaker notions of data extension and sketch a future research programme.
one_liner: Builds a formal framework for unsupervised representation learning directly on quantum-state data with latent quantum systems.
why_it_matters: If quantum devices produce coherent data streams, learning representations without first measuring them could become a core primitive for sensors, simulators, and networks.
detailed_summary: The paper models unsupervised learning from quantum data using joint quantum states over visible and latent systems, with inference and generation defined through state-over-time maps. It shows that consistent nontrivial models require nonlinear extended maps, then characterizes ambiguous states for three representative constructions. A key technical result is that the Leifer-Spekkens construction supports both inference and generation exactly for PPT model states, allowing quantum visible-latent correlations.
main_result: The authors characterize when quantum joint-state models admit inference and generation channels, identifying a PPT-linked hierarchy for representative state-over-time maps.
application_angle: The framework targets future quantum sensors and networks where useful structure may need to be extracted before destructive measurement.

title: Dual-polarized, mid-infrared nonreciprocal absorption
abstract: The emission and absorption of thermal radiation are usually coupled via Kirchhoff's law or reciprocity, stated as the equality of spectral directional emissivity and absorptivity. Magneto-optical materials have recently been identified as a promising route to lifting the constraint of reciprocity, with multiple experimental demonstrations using doped InAs. However, these demonstrations have been limited to p-polarized light in the Voigt configuration, whereas thermal radiation from a blackbody is unpolarized. Therefore, to break reciprocity in both polarization channels, we design a nanophotonic, dual-polarized nonreciprocal absorber operating in the mid-infrared spectral range (11-20 $\unicode{x03BC}$m), consisting of an a-Si photonic crystal slab on top of a doped InAs substrate described by an antisymmetric, nonreciprocal dielectric tensor under an applied magnetic field. The photonic crystal slab supports eigenmodes that couple to both s- and p-polarized light, resulting in absorption peaks that frequency shift in opposite directions for forward- and backward-propagating light$\unicode{x2014}$a signature of nonreciprocity in planar, subwavelength systems. We fabricate our design, then measure its room-temperature absorptance using magnetic-field-integrated absorptance spectroscopy, experimentally demonstrating nonreciprocal absorption for both polarizations. Our design is a step toward the complete control of light as heat, which could improve photonic energy conversion, thermal management, and mid-infrared optical isolation and circulation.
one_liner: Demonstrates mid-infrared nonreciprocal absorption for both s- and p-polarized light using a magneto-optical nanophotonic absorber.
why_it_matters: Dual-polarization nonreciprocity is important for real thermal radiation, which is generally unpolarized, and for practical mid-IR thermal photonics.
detailed_summary: The work designs and fabricates an amorphous-silicon photonic crystal slab on doped InAs under magnetic bias, exploiting the antisymmetric dielectric tensor of the substrate. The slab modes couple to both s- and p-polarized incident light, producing opposite frequency shifts for forward and backward propagation. Room-temperature magnetic-field-integrated absorptance spectroscopy verifies nonreciprocal absorption in both polarization channels over the 11-20 micrometer mid-infrared band.
platform_or_system: a-Si photonic crystal on doped InAs
main_result: The experiment demonstrates dual-polarized room-temperature mid-infrared nonreciprocal absorption in a planar subwavelength nanophotonic structure.
application_angle: This advances thermal emission control, mid-IR optical isolation or circulation, photonic energy conversion, and thermal management.

title: Feedback-Enhanced Quantum Metrology and Clock Precision under Thermodynamic Uncertainty
abstract: Feedback can convert continuously monitored quantum jumps into a thermodynamic resource. We formulate full counting statistics for open quantum systems under unital jump feedback by incorporating the feedback maps into the tilted generator. The resulting trajectory ensemble determines both current fluctuations and the Fisher information of the measurement record. We show that feedback can enhance reservoir-parameter estimation and clock precision without necessarily changing average thermodynamic currents. This enhanced precision is not bounded by reservoir entropy production alone. By embedding the reduced dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, we derive a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation in which the information entropy production of the feedback apparatus supplies the missing cost. A charge-monitored double quantum dot illustrates the framework: jump-conditioned feedback improves thermometry and chemical-potential sensing, and stabilizes a quantum clock defined by output-current ticks.
one_liner: Shows that jump-conditioned feedback can improve quantum sensing and clock precision beyond bounds based only on reservoir entropy production.
why_it_matters: It clarifies how measurement and feedback resources enter precision limits for monitored quantum devices used as sensors or clocks.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate full counting statistics for open quantum systems with unital jump feedback by inserting feedback maps into the tilted generator. They connect trajectory ensembles to current fluctuations and Fisher information, showing that feedback can enhance parameter estimation and clock precision without changing average currents. A feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation is derived by embedding the system in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, and a charge-monitored double quantum dot demonstrates improved thermometry, chemical-potential sensing, and output-current clock stabilization.
main_result: Jump-conditioned feedback improves reservoir-parameter estimation and quantum clock precision while revealing an additional information-entropy cost.
application_angle: The results guide practical feedback design for nanoscale quantum sensors and autonomous precision devices.

title: Parametric amplification of continuous-variable entangled state for loss-tolerant quantum distributed sensing
abstract: Quantum metrology exploits quantum states to achieve an estimation sensitivity beyond classical limits. In the continuous-variable (CV) regime, the squeezed state has been used to implement deterministic quantum sensing, but the quantum metrology sensitivity of this state is significantly affected by losses or detection inefficiencies, which restrict its applications. In this work, quantum distributed sensing is proposed using optical parametric amplified multimode entanglement generated from squeezed states. It is found that the sensitivity is robust to loss or detection inefficiency when large-gain optical parametric amplification (OPA) is introduced, where a two-mode Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen-entangled state and a four-mode cluster state are exploited for analysis. The quantum sensitivity is greatly improved compared to that without OPA in almost all loss scenarios. The quantum Fisher matrix is calculated for both states to obtain the optimal bound in comparison with our scheme, and it is found that even with a small or moderate OPA gain, quantum sensing can be improved compared with the traditional scheme. The states are also compared with corresponding single-mode squeezed states, finding the parameter ranges where entangled states perform better. This study provides a method for realizing large-scale quantum metrology in real-world applications despite losses or detection inefficiencies.
one_liner: Proposes optical parametric amplification of CV entangled states to make distributed quantum sensing more tolerant to loss.
why_it_matters: Loss and detector inefficiency are major barriers for deploying squeezed-light and CV-entanglement metrology outside ideal lab conditions.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes distributed sensing with multimode continuous-variable entanglement generated from squeezed states and boosted by optical parametric amplification. It studies two-mode EPR states and four-mode cluster states, calculating quantum Fisher matrices and comparing practical schemes with optimal bounds. Large-gain OPA makes sensitivity robust against loss or detection inefficiency, while even small or moderate gain improves performance over traditional schemes in broad regimes.
main_result: The study shows that parametric amplification can substantially improve loss-tolerant sensitivity for CV distributed sensing with EPR and cluster states.
application_angle: The approach is relevant to scalable optical quantum metrology networks where channel loss and detector inefficiency are unavoidable.

title: The Fermionic Cohomology Problem on the Full Fock Space Is $\mathrm{QMA}_1$-Complete
abstract: Fermionic cohomology characterizes the zero-energy states of the supersymmetric Hamiltonian associated with a fermionic differential. Previous work showed that the problem restricted to a particle-number sector specified with the input is $\mathrm{QMA}_1$-hard and belongs to $\mathrm{QMA}$.
