detailed_summary: The paper controls dipolar many-body dynamics in an ensemble of about 10000 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond using pulsed magnetic-field gradients. It reports practical gains of 7.9(2) dB for magnetic signal detection and 8.8(3) dB for magnetic noise sensing, including overheads. The same control enables momentum-space-resolved sensing of spatially correlated magnetic noise with tunable length scales down to 50 nm.
main_result: Demonstrates overhead-inclusive metrological gain and spatially resolved magnetic-noise sensing down to 50 nm length scales.
application_angle: The technique is directly relevant to nanoscale biological imaging and magnetic materials characterization.

title: Stabilization of dark states in emitter arrays coupled to a half-waveguide
abstract: The radiative properties of quantum emitters are profoundly influenced by their electromagnetic environment. When coupled to a waveguide terminated at one end by a mirror, distant emitters interact strongly via virtual photon exchange, leading to collective superradiant and subradiant states with enhanced or suppressed decay rates. We demonstrate that applying optimal frequency shifts to each emitter enables the formation of perfect single-excitation dark states (i.e. states with zero decay rate) and near-perfect multi-excitation dark states in small ensembles. These collective states can be deterministically prepared with high fidelity using classical driving fields or few-photon pulses propagating along the waveguide. These results, readily implementable in superconducting qubit platforms, open new avenues for quantum information storage, networking and control of light.
one_liner: Stabilizes perfect and near-perfect dark states in emitter arrays coupled to a mirrored half-waveguide.
why_it_matters: Controllable subradiant states are useful for quantum memories, networking, and waveguide-QED light-matter interfaces.
detailed_summary: The study considers quantum emitters coupled to a waveguide terminated by a mirror, where virtual-photon exchange produces collective radiative modes. By applying optimized emitter frequency shifts, the authors form perfect single-excitation dark states and near-perfect multi-excitation dark states in small arrays. They also show high-fidelity deterministic preparation using classical drives or few-photon waveguide pulses.
main_result: Shows optimized local frequency shifts can create zero-decay single-excitation dark states and highly subradiant multi-excitation states.
application_angle: The approach could improve photonic quantum memories and networking nodes, especially in superconducting waveguide-QED hardware.

title: Robust Hamiltonian engineering with subensemble control
abstract: We present a robust protocol to reshape interactions in a spin ensemble based on global control pulse sequences applied to multiple subensembles in parallel. This setting arises naturally from ensembles of solid-state defects or multi-species atomic arrays. We show that it is provably computationally hard to find pulse sequences that simultaneously engineer interactions both within and between subensembles. Despite its formal hardness, we identify a set of necessary or sufficient conditions under which one can synthesize a target Hamiltonian from the native one. Moreover, we introduce efficient numerical strategies for designing pulse sequences that engineer target Hamiltonians robust against common control imperfections. As a specific application, we discuss the robust generation of two-mode spin squeezing in dual-species atomic ensembles, which is a challenging task without subensemble control. Our results provide a practical toolbox to design novel quantum simulation and sensing experiments with minimal control overhead.
one_liner: Develops subensemble pulse-control methods for robust Hamiltonian engineering in spin ensembles.
why_it_matters: It provides a practical route to programmable interactions with low control overhead in defect ensembles and multi-species atomic arrays.
detailed_summary: The paper studies how global pulse sequences applied to multiple subensembles can reshape native interactions within and between spin groups. It proves the general synthesis problem is computationally hard, then derives useful necessary or sufficient conditions for reachable target Hamiltonians. Efficient numerical design strategies are introduced to make the engineered interactions robust against common pulse imperfections, with two-mode spin squeezing as a target application.
main_result: Provides constructive and numerical protocols for robustly synthesizing target spin Hamiltonians under subensemble control.
application_angle: Robust low-overhead interaction engineering can support quantum simulation, squeezing-enhanced sensing, and defect-based experiments.

title: Resource-adaptive distributed fault tolerance with very noisy Bell pairs
abstract: Distributed architectures have been proposed as a pathway to large-scale quantum computers. Combined with the need for fault-tolerance, such architectures require distributed quantum error correction (DQEC) and distributed logical gates. An important challenge is how to realize DQEC primitives in the setting where interaction between modules is restricted to shared Bell pairs that are significantly noisier than on-chip operations. We extend the framework known as fault tolerance by construction to this setting, deriving different strategies for handling the additional noise. Through fault-improvement we recover conventional entanglement distillation, and also find more dynamical protocols that enable space-time trade-offs. We show that integrated decoding halves the required distillation code distance compared to entanglement distillation implemented using separate decoding, thus requiring significantly fewer Bell pairs. As a main focus of the work, we synthesize efficient circuits for an important primitive in distributed fault tolerance: distributed stabilizer measurements. These circuits can be adapted to resource constraints, e.g. on the Bell pair generation rate or the space available for on-chip auxiliary qubits. Noting that full local fault-tolerance is not always needed to preserve the correct scaling of logical error rates, we further optimize the circuits depending on the surrounding context. We consider in particular the surface code and the color code, both as distributed memories and in the case of lattice surgery across separate modules. Here, robustness to certain hook and readout errors reduces the number of required Bell pairs even further, compared to the context-free setting. We numerically benchmark the resulting implementations under circuit level noise with additional interconnect noise.
one_liner: Designs distributed fault-tolerance primitives that adapt to very noisy inter-module Bell pairs.
why_it_matters: Distributed quantum computers need efficient ways to tolerate poor interconnect fidelity without excessive Bell-pair and auxiliary-qubit overhead.
detailed_summary: The paper extends fault tolerance by construction to distributed architectures where modules share Bell pairs much noisier than local operations. It compares fault-improvement, entanglement distillation, integrated decoding, and dynamic space-time trade-offs for distributed QEC primitives. The authors synthesize resource-adaptive circuits for distributed stabilizer measurements and benchmark them under circuit-level noise with added interconnect noise for surface-code and color-code settings.
main_result: Shows integrated decoding can halve the distillation code distance and reduces Bell-pair needs for distributed stabilizer measurements.
application_angle: The circuits inform scalable modular quantum-computer designs constrained by slow or noisy photonic interconnects.

title: Multi-Boundary Many-Body Quantum Teleportation
abstract: Unlike standard quantum teleportation, many-body teleportation uses scrambling to transmit quantum information. In this protocol, initially localized information spreads over many degrees of freedom and is later refocused at the receiver by a simple coupling between the systems, followed by further many-body evolution. The protocol was developed from models of traversable wormholes in holography and has become a useful probe of scrambling. In particular, it can distinguish genuine scrambling from decoherence or noise when out-of-time-order correlators fail, and can reveal signatures of different scrambling mechanisms, including the distinctive behavior expected in holographic systems. Holography predicts that related protocols can transmit information between selected boundaries of multi-boundary wormhole geometries. Motivated by this setting, we study single-qubit many-body teleportation among three systems of qubits. The initial state consists of EPR pairs distributed among them, providing a simple analogue of an infinite-temperature three-boundary holographic state. We analyze the protocol with one-dimensional and all-to-all dynamics, both analytically and numerically using random circuits. We find that the third system suppresses teleportation once the spreading message reaches the region of qubits that are entangled with it. In one dimension, both the minimum coupling required for successful teleportation and the fidelity depend on the distance from the injection site to this region, a feature reminiscent of holographic causal shadows. For all-to-all dynamics, successful teleportation is instead restricted to early times and to sufficiently few qubits entangled with the third system. A third system therefore provides spatial, or subsystem, resolution of information spreading that is absent from the two-sided protocol. Our results offer a step toward many-body teleportation networks.
one_liner: Extends many-body teleportation to three coupled qubit systems, using a third boundary to spatially resolve scrambling and information flow.
why_it_matters: It turns many-body teleportation from a two-system scrambling probe into a network-like diagnostic for where quantum information spreads.
detailed_summary: The paper studies single-qubit many-body teleportation among three qubit systems initialized with EPR-pair structure analogous to a three-boundary holographic state. Analytical and random-circuit simulations show that the third system suppresses teleportation once the encoded message reaches qubits entangled with it. In one-dimensional dynamics, the required coupling and fidelity depend on the distance to this third-system-entangled region, while all-to-all dynamics allow only early-time operation with limited third-system entanglement.
main_result: A third qubit system provides subsystem-resolved control and suppression of many-body teleportation depending on information-spreading geometry.
application_angle: The protocol could become a diagnostic tool for scrambling, decoherence discrimination, and networked quantum-information transfer in controllable many-body platforms.

title: Optimized Matrix-Product State Simulations of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
abstract: Simulating quantum error correction (QEC) circuits including non-Clifford gates at scale is important to accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. Here we demonstrate that matrix product state (MPS) techniques can handle many QEC circuits exactly and without restriction on gate types. Crucially, we find that MPS efficiency depends sensitively on implementation choices, and we introduce a series of targeted optimizations that reduce bond dimensions and simulation time by several orders of magnitude compared to naive approaches. We illustrate this with examples including: (a) a rotated surface code quantum memory up to distance 11, (b) logical Bell-state preparation up to distance 9, (c) a 15-to-1 magic-state distillation circuit including hundreds of QEC rounds that we optimize to be simulated with only 11 logical qubits (187 physical qubits) and a maximal bond dimension of 64 in under 40 seconds, and (d) a narrow, deep random circuit that scales linearly with the number of T gates. These results demonstrate the importance of circuit-level optimizations and position MPS as a valuable complement to near-Clifford simulators for QEC circuits.
one_liner: Shows optimized MPS methods can exactly simulate large QEC circuits with non-Clifford gates far faster than naive tensor-network approaches.
why_it_matters: Efficient exact simulation helps validate near-term fault-tolerant circuits, including magic-state distillation, beyond Clifford-only tooling.
detailed_summary: The work introduces circuit-level matrix-product-state optimizations that reduce bond dimension and runtime for quantum error-correction simulations. Demonstrations include rotated surface-code memory to distance 11, logical Bell-state preparation to distance 9, and a 15-to-1 magic-state distillation circuit compressed to 11 logical qubits and 187 physical qubits. The distillation example runs with maximum bond dimension 64 in under 40 seconds, showing that implementation choices dominate practical MPS performance.
main_result: Optimized MPS simulations handle exact QEC circuits with arbitrary gates, including deep non-Clifford workloads, at practical scale.
application_angle: This provides a useful verification and design tool for early fault-tolerant architectures where full state-vector simulation is infeasible.

title: Deterministic nanofabrication for engineering nanowire quantum dot devices
abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are a leading platform for realising bright, wavelength-tunable sources of single and entangled photon pairs for photonic quantum technologies. Site-selected nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) are a promising platform for fabricating such photonic devices in a scalable manner. However, implementing additional structures around the photonic nanowire while maintaining its vertical growth geometry has remained a challenge. In this work, we develop a deterministic pick-and-place technique to conduct a vertical-to-vertical transfer of NWQDs from the growth substrate to arbitrary templates. Using this transfer technique, we enhance the photon extraction efficiency to 75% by implementing a bottom gold mirror and tune the emission wavelength by 3.6 GHz via implementing electrostatic gates around the QD. Importantly, we measure low-multiphoton probability (g^(2)(0) = 0.002) and high indistinguishability (>80% for +/-100 ps) of the QD emission after the transfer process, yielding high-quality devices. These results demonstrate the repeatability and versatility of the developed transfer technique, which is an enabling step towards scalable single and entangled photon sources.
one_liner: Demonstrates deterministic vertical transfer of nanowire quantum dots onto device templates while preserving high-quality single-photon emission.
why_it_matters: It addresses a key fabrication bottleneck for scalable quantum-dot photon sources with mirrors, gates, and engineered photonic structures.
detailed_summary: The authors develop a pick-and-place method that transfers site-selected nanowire quantum dots from the growth substrate to arbitrary templates while keeping the nanowire vertical. A bottom gold mirror raises photon extraction efficiency to 75%, and electrostatic gates tune the emission by 3.6 GHz. After transfer, the devices retain low multiphoton probability with g2(0)=0.002 and more than 80% photon indistinguishability over +/-100 ps.
main_result: Transferred nanowire quantum dots achieve 75% extraction efficiency, GHz-scale electrostatic tuning, g2(0)=0.002, and high indistinguishability.
application_angle: The method supports scalable fabrication of bright, tunable single-photon and entangled-photon sources for photonic quantum technologies.

title: Non-Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Quantum Sensors for Quantum Parameter Estimation
abstract: Non-KAM (Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser) systems, when subjected to weak time-dependent perturbations, exhibit an abrupt transition to classical chaos through the breakdown of invariant phase-space tori. We showcase the utilization of non-KAM systems in the quantum regime as quantum sensors, leveraging their sensitivity at \textit{resonances}. Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a central quantity in quantum parameter estimation theory that measures how much information a quantum state contains about an unknown parameter that is encoded into it. In other words, it quantifies the sensitivity of a quantum state to small changes in that parameter. In this work, through numerical analysis in conjunction with analytical results, we study the performance of the non-KAM systems for quantum sensing applications by computing the QFI. We find that the growth of the QFI is remarkably enhanced when the resonance condition is satisfied. For frequency estimation under Floquet unitary encodings, we derive a transport bound: if the mean excitation number grows as $\langle\hat n(t)\rangle\sim t^α$, the QFI obeys $I(t)\lesssim t^{2α+2}$. The quantum kicked harmonic oscillator, a paradigmatic non-KAM system, realizes the full hierarchy: localized dynamics ($α=0$) yield quadratic growth, delocalized diffusion along stochastic webs ($α=1$) yields quartic growth, and translationally invariant resonances ($α=2$) saturate the bound with anomalous hexic growth, $I(t)\sim t^{6}$, established analytically at resonance $R=2$ and numerically at $R=4$. The enhancement stems from resonance-induced translational symmetry rather than exponential instability, identifying non-KAM resonances as a metrological resource distinct from chaos-assisted and criticality-based sensing.
one_liner: Proposes non-KAM resonant quantum dynamics as a sensing resource with QFI growth up to hexic scaling in kicked harmonic oscillators.
why_it_matters: It identifies resonance-induced transport, rather than chaos alone, as a route to strongly enhanced quantum parameter estimation.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes quantum parameter estimation in non-KAM systems under weak time-dependent perturbations, focusing on resonant enhancement of quantum Fisher information. For Floquet frequency estimation, it derives a transport bound linking mean excitation growth <n(t)>~t^alpha to QFI scaling I(t)<=t^(2alpha+2). The kicked harmonic oscillator realizes quadratic, quartic, and hexic QFI growth regimes, with I(t)~t^6 established analytically at resonance R=2 and numerically at R=4.
main_result: Non-KAM resonances can produce anomalously fast QFI growth, including hexic scaling under translationally invariant resonant dynamics.
application_angle: The mechanism suggests tunable high-sensitivity Floquet sensors based on resonant transport in controllable quantum dynamical systems.

title: Experimental validation of a compact fault-tolerant architecture for trapped ions
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is beginning to enable logical operations that outperform their unencoded physical counterparts, but useful fault-tolerant computation will require more than low-error quantum memory. An effective architecture must orchestrate efficient logical encoding, low-overhead logical operations, and access to the non-Clifford resources required for universal computation. Here, we introduce and experimentally validate such an architecture based on the $[[20,2,6]]$ $C_4$-Helix code, designed for the early fault-tolerant regime. Using Quantinuum Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor, we experimentally demonstrate the principal components of this architecture: we perform repeated quantum error correction with an error of $4.6^{+6.2}_{-2.6}\times10^{-5}$ per logical qubit per QEC cycle. We benchmark the complete Clifford group on the two logical qubits of a single codeblock under active error correction, obtaining an error of $2.8^{+1.0}_{-1.6}\times 10^{-4}$ per two-qubit logical Clifford. We further demonstrate a fault-tolerant chain-map interface between $C_4$-Helix and a distance-5 surface code, preparing a heterogeneous three-logical-qubit GHZ state with a fidelity lower bound of $99.925^{+0.068}_{-0.245}\%$. In each case, the encoded implementation outperforms its corresponding unencoded physical baseline without relying on postselection. Circuit-level simulations indicate that improvements in physical fidelity bring the same architecture into the $10^{-6}$-$10^{-8}$ logical-error regime targeted for early fault-tolerant computation. Together, these results establish $C_4$-Helix as a hardware-validated fault-tolerant architecture rather than a bare quantum memory.
one_liner: Experimentally validates a compact trapped-ion fault-tolerant architecture using the [[20,2,6]] C4-Helix code on Quantinuum Helios.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates active QEC, logical Clifford operations, and code interfacing with encoded performance beating physical baselines without postselection.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements the [[20,2,6]] C4-Helix code on a 98-qubit trapped-ion processor and validates core pieces of an early fault-tolerant architecture. Repeated QEC reaches an error of 4.6e-5 per logical qubit per QEC cycle, and the full two-logical-qubit Clifford group is benchmarked at 2.8e-4 error per logical Clifford under active correction. A fault-tolerant chain-map interface to a distance-5 surface code prepares a heterogeneous three-logical-qubit GHZ state with a 99.925% fidelity lower bound.
main_result: The C4-Helix architecture performs active QEC, logical Clifford operations, and heterogeneous code interfacing with encoded advantage over physical baselines.
application_angle: This is a hardware-level step toward low-overhead early fault-tolerant computation with realistic logical operations beyond memory protection.

title: Tunable topological enhancement of covariant quantum Fisher information via non-Bloch skin effect in non-Hermitian SSH lattices
abstract: The covariant quantum Fisher information (CQFI) has recently been established as the ultimate precision benchmark for pseudo-Hermitian sensors [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 080802 (2026)], yet existing analyses are limited to single-mode systems. Here we extend the CQFI formalism to multi-mode non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattices and reveal tunable topological enhancement enabled by the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). Under open boundary conditions, the NHSE deforms the conventional Brillouin zone into a generalized Brillouin zone of radius r = exp(\k{appa}), where \k{appa} denotes the non-Bloch decay rate. While the total CQFI scales linearly with system size N, its prefactor depends critically on \k{appa}, yielding an enhancement factor E(N) = F_OBC / F_PBC that exceeds 30 for N ~ 30, substantially outperforming periodic-boundary sensors. The enhancement is robust against moderate local disorder and supports multi-parameter estimation, with the joint Cramér-Rao bound reduced by up to 15 orders of magnitude. These findings establish a spatial-domain mechanism for quantum metrology that complements time-domain strategies and is experimentally accessible using topoelectrical circuits, photonic lattices, and superconducting circuits with current technology.
one_liner: Extends covariant QFI to non-Hermitian SSH lattices and shows tunable topological enhancement from the non-Bloch skin effect.
why_it_matters: It gives a spatial-domain route to enhanced quantum sensing that is compatible with photonic, circuit, and superconducting lattice platforms.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes covariant quantum Fisher information to multi-mode pseudo-Hermitian non-Hermitian SSH lattices. Under open boundaries, the non-Hermitian skin effect reshapes the generalized Brillouin zone and enhances the CQFI prefactor while total CQFI remains linear in system size. The reported enhancement exceeds 30 for N around 30, is robust to moderate local disorder, and can reduce joint Cramer-Rao bounds by up to 15 orders of magnitude in multi-parameter estimation.
main_result: Open-boundary non-Hermitian SSH lattices provide tunable CQFI enhancement through skin-effect-induced spatial mode localization.
application_angle: The approach is experimentally relevant for topoelectrical circuits, photonic lattices, and superconducting circuits used as precision sensors.

title: Universal scaling of fluctuations and correlations across the superfluid transition
abstract: The critical behavior of a system near a continuous phase transition is commonly characterized by power laws and a set of universal critical exponents. Yet universality at phase transitions has even more fundamental manifestations. It dictates that all observables follow universal scaling functions, which may extend beyond simple power laws. Furthermore, microscopic details are captured entirely by only two system-specific scale factors, that rescale any measured quantity onto its universal form. In this work, we report the experimental validation of this prediction in ultracold lattice Bose gases undergoing the superfluid transition. We extract the scale factors by collapsing the order-parameter cumulants measured at varying entropies. We show that these factors specify scaling functions governing both the order-parameter distribution and two-point correlations. By measuring these scaling functions, we also determine three critical exponents $β$, $γ$ and $ν$. Our results provide an experimental demonstration that universal scaling is simultaneously obeyed by multiple observables in a quantum many-body system.
one_liner: Ultracold lattice Bose gases show universal scaling of fluctuations and correlations through the superfluid transition.
why_it_matters: It experimentally validates multi-observable universal scaling in a controllable quantum many-body platform, useful for benchmarking quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: The experiment studies ultracold lattice Bose gases near the superfluid transition and collapses order-parameter cumulants measured at different entropies. Two system-specific scale factors are extracted and then used to predict scaling functions for the full order-parameter distribution and two-point correlations. The measurements also yield critical exponents beta, gamma, and nu, demonstrating that multiple observables obey the same universal scaling framework.
main_result: The work demonstrates universal scaling functions for order-parameter fluctuations and correlations across the superfluid transition.
application_angle: The result strengthens cold-atom quantum simulators as quantitative platforms for testing critical phenomena beyond simple power-law fits.

title: Topology-Dependent Enhancement of Entanglement Extraction in Repeater Graph States
abstract: Quantum repeaters are essential for establishing long-distance quantum communication to overcome the exponential decay of entanglement due to photon loss. Traditional repeater architectures rely on physical quantum memory, which introduces decoherence and poses significant practical implementation challenges. The repeater graph state (RGS) architecture offers a promising memory-less alternative that is inherently resilient to photon losses. A key challenge in implementing RGS lies in the requirement for highly efficient graph state generators and complex qubit measurement. In this work, we aim to investigate the strategies for extracting the maximum number of Bell pairs from the RGS structure via its qubit connection to resolve the well-known bottleneck problem of RGS in which only a single Bell pair can be extracted from a complete bipartite graph state. From simulations, we observe that the maximum number of extracted Bell pairs depends on its connection topology, where the Bell-pair yield tends to be maximal at low to moderate edge densities. As the number of network hops increases, the RGS must be equipped with higher inner-qubit connectivity to maintain a sufficient yield of extractable Bell pairs. Thus, the expected resource requirement shifts toward the use of RGSs with higher inner-qubit connectivity.
one_liner: Simulations show that repeater graph state topology controls how many Bell pairs can be extracted for memoryless quantum repeaters.
why_it_matters: It targets a concrete resource bottleneck in graph-state quantum repeaters by linking Bell-pair yield to graph connectivity and hop count.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes repeater graph states as a memoryless alternative to conventional quantum repeaters with physical quantum memories. Through simulations, it studies how different connection topologies affect the maximum number of Bell pairs extractable from the graph. The results indicate that low to moderate edge densities can maximize yield, while longer network paths require higher inner-qubit connectivity to sustain performance.
main_result: The main result is that Bell-pair extraction yield is topology-dependent and can exceed the single-pair bottleneck under suitable connectivity.
application_angle: The analysis informs graph-state generator design for long-distance quantum communication with reduced reliance on long-lived memories.

title: Heralded one-, two- and three-photon states from waveguided parametric down-conversion
abstract: The manifold coincidences and singles counting provides a resource-saving quantum-optics analysis tool, since it is appropriate even in the presence of heavy experimental imperfections. Here, we prepare cross-polarized twin beams in the telecommunication wavelength range via parametric down-conversion in a periodically-poled KTiOPO$_4$ waveguide and herald photon-number states up to three photons. First, we show that the single-click probability is a versatile tool not only for extracting the state's mean photon number but also for sampling values of the moment generating function being the core behind any quantum optical state. Second, we measure values of the normalized factorial moments of photon number, $g^{(m)}_{\text{h}}$, up to the order $m = n+1$ for the heralded $n$-photon state. These normalized photon correlations provide an expedient method for examining the higher-order non-classicality of light by violating the condition $g^{(m+1)}_{\text{h}} \ge g^{(m)}_{\text{h}} \ge 1$.
one_liner: Waveguided PDC at telecom wavelengths heralds one-, two-, and three-photon states and verifies higher-order nonclassicality.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a compact telecom-band source and practical diagnostics for multiphoton states under realistic experimental imperfections.
detailed_summary: The experiment generates cross-polarized twin beams in a periodically poled KTiOPO4 waveguide and heralds photon-number states up to three photons. It uses manifold coincidences and singles counting to extract mean photon number and sample moment-generating-function values. Normalized factorial moments up to order n+1 are measured for heralded n-photon states, revealing violations of classical photon-correlation inequalities.
main_result: The work prepares telecom-band heralded one-, two-, and three-photon states and measures higher-order photon correlations confirming nonclassicality.
application_angle: Such compact heralded multiphoton sources and robust diagnostics are relevant for photonic quantum information and quantum communication experiments.

title: Pulse-Controlled Topologically Protected Quantum Batteries
abstract: Quantum batteries have emerged as a promising new generation of energy-storage devices for powering quantum technologies. Long-distance charging is particularly attractive because it minimizes interference between the charger and the battery, thereby attracting considerable interest. Here, we propose a topologically protected long-distance charging protocol for quantum batteries based on a pulse-controlled superconducting qubit chain. By dynamically modulating the pulse-mediated couplings, we realize topologically protected energy transfer from the charger to the battery. We show that the charging process is free of energy backflow and remains robust against imperfections in pulse control. Moreover, the energy stored in the battery at the target time is fully extractable, and the protocol remains effective for relatively large system sizes. To further accelerate charging, we optimize the pulse shape and elucidate the underlying physical mechanism. Our pulse-controlled topological quantum battery protocol provides a versatile framework for implementing long-distance topological charging and establishes a theoretical foundation for designing optimal-control strategies to enhance quantum battery performance.
one_liner: A pulse-controlled superconducting qubit chain is proposed for robust topological long-distance charging of quantum batteries.
why_it_matters: It connects topological protection and optimal pulse control to energy transfer in superconducting quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a long-distance quantum battery charging protocol using a pulse-controlled superconducting qubit chain. Dynamically modulated couplings produce topologically protected energy transfer from charger to battery without energy backflow. The stored energy is reported to be fully extractable at the target time, robust to pulse imperfections, and improvable through pulse-shape optimization.
main_result: The main result is a theoretical protocol for robust, backflow-free, topologically protected long-distance charging.
application_angle: The protocol could guide control strategies for energy management and state transfer in superconducting quantum devices.

title: Enhancing noise robustness in device-independent conference key agreement with asymmetric parity-CHSH inequalities
abstract: Conference key agreement allows multiple remote parties to establish a shared secret key with information-theoretical security. In device-independent conference key agreement, security can be guaranteed with minimal assumptions on the devices used, provided that a violation of a Bell inequality is observed. However, implementations are extremely challenging because high detection efficiency is required to observe loophole-free Bell violations. Here, we enhance the robustness of device-independent conference key agreement by introducing a new family of multipartite Bell inequalities called the asymmetric parity-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequalities. We derive a tight analytical lower bound on the conditional von Neumann entropy of the outcomes of one of the parties in a protocol based on this inequality, including noisy preprocessing. Using this bound, we analyze robustness to detection inefficiencies as well as local and global depolarizing noise. We show that the combination of the asymmetric parity-CHSH inequality and noisy preprocessing can significantly improve the robustness to imperfections.
one_liner: Asymmetric parity-CHSH inequalities improve noise tolerance for device-independent conference key agreement.
why_it_matters: It advances practical multiparty quantum cryptography by reducing sensitivity to detection inefficiency and depolarizing noise.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces asymmetric parity-CHSH inequalities for multipartite device-independent conference key agreement. It derives a tight analytical lower bound on the conditional von Neumann entropy for one party's outcomes, including the effect of noisy preprocessing. Using this bound, the authors evaluate robustness against detector inefficiency and local or global depolarizing noise, finding significant tolerance improvements.
main_result: The work shows that asymmetric parity-CHSH inequalities plus noisy preprocessing can substantially improve imperfection tolerance.
application_angle: Improved robustness is directly relevant to photonic implementations of device-independent multiparty secure communication.

title: Optimizing Atom Transport, Gate-Count and Depth with Parity Twine
abstract: We present an efficient implementation of the Parity Architecture for neutral-atom quantum processors. We adapt Parity Twine Networks (PTNs) to different atom layouts, native entangling gates, and atom-shuttling capabilities. This provides a general framework for hardware-aware optimization of gate count, circuit depth, and atom transport for quantum circuits encoding arbitrary interaction graphs in a common basis. Specifically, we develop PTN constructions based on different native entangling-gate realizations, namely CZ, CZSWAP, and iSWAP, providing flexibility to accommodate different hardware capabilities on both static and mobile neutral-atom platforms. Using the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) as a representative example, we demonstrate substantial reductions in two-qubit gate count, atom transport, and circuit depth. These resource savings translate into an estimated circuit fidelity three orders of magnitude higher than competing compilation strategies for a 30-qubit QFT. We further extend the construction to the recently introduced optimistic QFT and discuss the broader applicability of PTNs to other quantum algorithms on neutral-atom platforms.
one_liner: Parity Twine Networks are adapted to neutral-atom processors to reduce gates, depth, transport, and estimated QFT infidelity.
why_it_matters: It gives hardware-aware compilation methods for neutral-atom quantum processors with large projected fidelity gains.
detailed_summary: The paper presents implementations of the Parity Architecture for neutral-atom quantum processors using Parity Twine Networks. It adapts constructions to atom layouts, native gates including CZ, CZSWAP, and iSWAP, and different shuttling capabilities. For QFT and optimistic QFT circuits, the approach reduces two-qubit gate count, transport, and depth, with an estimated three-order-of-magnitude fidelity improvement for a 30-qubit QFT compared with competing strategies.
main_result: The main demonstrated capability is hardware-aware PTN compilation that substantially reduces resources for interaction-graph circuits such as QFT.
application_angle: The method is practical for improving executable circuit quality on static and mobile neutral-atom hardware.

title: Low-Frequency Charge Noise in Bilayer Graphene Quantum Dots
abstract: Bilayer graphene (BLG) quantum dots (QDs) are a promising platform for semiconductor qubits. However, the low-frequency charge noise that may ultimately limit coherence has remained largely unexplored. Here, we systematically characterize charge noise in gate-defined BLG QDs using transport-based noise spectroscopy. We extract a median amplitude of $ S_μ^{1/2} (1~\text{Hz}) = 1.16~μ\text{eV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, placing BLG well within the range reported for established semiconductor quantum-dot platforms. Across variations in charge occupation, confinement, source-drain bias, and charge-sensor operating conditions, neither the noise amplitude nor the spectral dependence shows a reproducible trend in electrostatic tuning, indicating that we extracted the intrinsic semiconductor noise. Consistent noise levels are further observed in double QDs and confirmed using an independent superconducting resonator-based dispersive readout. Extending the study to BLG devices incorporating transition metal dichalcogenide layers reveals no measurable charge noise increase in weakly proximitized QDs. These results validate BLG as a viable platform for coherent quantum information processing.
one_liner: Transport and resonator readout show bilayer graphene quantum dots have low intrinsic charge noise comparable to mature semiconductor qubits.
why_it_matters: Charge noise is a key coherence limiter, so quantifying BLG noise under realistic tuning validates it as a serious semiconductor-qubit platform.
detailed_summary: The work systematically measures low-frequency charge noise in gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum dots using transport-based noise spectroscopy. It reports a median 1 Hz noise amplitude of 1.16 micro-eV/sqrt(Hz), with no reproducible dependence on occupation, confinement, bias, or sensor settings. Similar behavior is observed in double dots and independently confirmed by superconducting-resonator dispersive readout, while weak TMD proximity does not measurably increase noise.
main_result: BLG quantum dots exhibit intrinsic low-frequency charge noise within the range of established semiconductor quantum-dot qubit platforms.
application_angle: The result supports BLG as a practical host for coherent spin or valley qubits, including hybrid devices with proximitizing layers.

title: Fractalizing spacetime: Floquet codes with fractonic excitations that are immobile in space and time
abstract: We generalize fractalization, a procedure for the construction of fracton models, from space to spacetime. We apply spacetime fractalization to construct fracton floquet codes with syndrome excitations that have limited mobility in space and time. This extends the notion of fracton order to intrinsically dynamical quantum phases of matter that are inequivalent to static fracton phases. We find spacetime type-II fracton floquet codes which have no topological excitations that are mobile in space or time. These codes exhibit an extreme form of quantum discrete time crystal order with response periods that scale exponentially in their linear system sizes. In this context, the no-strings rule that characterizes type-II fractons leads to a superlinear scaling of the floquet code fault-distance with time, potentially lowering the time overhead required for quantum error correction.
one_liner: Spacetime fractalization yields Floquet codes whose syndrome excitations are constrained in both space and time.
why_it_matters: The construction links dynamical fracton order to quantum error correction and suggests fault-distance scaling that could reduce temporal overhead.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes fractalization from spatial lattices to spacetime and uses it to construct fracton Floquet codes. The resulting type-II dynamical codes can lack topological excitations mobile in either space or time. They also exhibit discrete time-crystal responses with periods growing exponentially in system size, and the no-strings structure gives superlinear Floquet-code fault-distance scaling with time.
main_result: A class of intrinsically dynamical fracton Floquet codes is constructed with immobile spacetime excitations and favorable fault-distance behavior.
application_angle: These codes may inform quantum-memory architectures where temporal error-correction overhead is a central hardware constraint.

title: Analog quantum simulation of bosonic and anyonic models with flux-driven transmons
abstract: When quantum particles interact, many-body phenomena that are hard to simulate classically emerge. Quantum analog simulation offers an alternative in which the target system's dynamics is directly realized in controllable quantum hardware. Here, we give a general protocol for simulating the Bose-Hubbard and anyon-Hubbard models using lattices of capacitively coupled flux-tunable transmons. By modulating the transmon frequencies in an alternating pattern, we resonantly drive multiple many-body transitions and can tune the on-site interaction and density-dependent hopping amplitudes for up to three bosons per site, with no additional restriction on the total particle number. By adding phases to the modulation, which renders the transition amplitudes complex-valued, we propose the first simulation protocol for the anyon-Hubbard model with transmons. Numerical simulations of the driven transmon arrays with experimentally realistic parameters reproduce the characteristic dynamics of the target models across a range of interaction strengths and statistical phases, including the interaction-dependent localization and the statistics-dependent asymmetry of the anyonic quantum walk.
one_liner: Flux-driven transmon arrays are proposed as analog simulators for Bose-Hubbard and anyon-Hubbard dynamics.
why_it_matters: It gives a hardware-realistic route to anyonic lattice physics using tunable superconducting circuits rather than specialized particles.
detailed_summary: The authors present a protocol for simulating Bose-Hubbard and anyon-Hubbard models in capacitively coupled flux-tunable transmon lattices. Alternating frequency modulation resonantly drives many-body transitions and tunes on-site interactions plus density-dependent hopping for up to three bosons per site. Adding modulation phases makes transition amplitudes complex, enabling anyon-Hubbard behavior; numerical simulations with realistic parameters reproduce localization and statistics-dependent quantum-walk asymmetry.
main_result: Realistic driven transmon lattices can emulate bosonic and anyonic Hubbard dynamics with tunable interactions and statistical phases.
application_angle: The protocol expands superconducting-circuit simulators toward experimentally accessible studies of strongly correlated and anyonic transport.

title: Energetic Costs of Subspace Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction acts as an entropy pump, transferring noise-induced uncertainty from a protected quantum system into syndrome information stored in an auxiliary memory. Repeated operation requires this memory to be cleared which unavoidably contributes to the energetic cost of error correction. Here, we characterise this contribution for subspace quantum error-correcting codes and identify how it depends on the joint structure of the code, the noise, and the representation of the retained syndrome information. Starting from the Knill-Laflamme conditions, we construct an effective syndrome state whose von Neumann entropy sets a lower bound on the ideal work required to maintain a reusable syndrome register. Projective syndrome readout generally generates additional entropy, and we quantify the resulting gap through measurement inefficiency. We then specialise to stabiliser codes under independent local Pauli noise and analyse two classical levels of syndrome representation. At the level of abstract error labels, degeneracies among single-qubit errors reduce the leading-order entropy of processed recovery labels. At the parity-check level, lower-weight checks reduce the marginal entropy generated by individual measurement outcomes in the low-noise regime. We identify the additional burden associated with retaining and separately erasing these outcomes as a bit-level inefficiency, and illustrate both costs for the five-qubit, Steane, generalised Shor, and rotated surface codes. Our results establish a hierarchy of syndrome-memory energetic costs and identify the code, noise, and measurement structures that control the ideal thermodynamic burden of subspace quantum error correction.
one_liner: The paper derives thermodynamic lower bounds for repeatedly erasing syndrome information in subspace quantum error correction.
why_it_matters: As QEC scales, syndrome acquisition and reset become physical resource costs, not just abstract circuit steps.
detailed_summary: Starting from Knill-Laflamme conditions, the work defines an effective syndrome state whose von Neumann entropy lower-bounds the ideal work needed to reset reusable syndrome memory. It separates entropy intrinsic to retained syndrome information from extra entropy produced by projective readout and measurement representation. For stabilizer codes under local Pauli noise, it compares abstract recovery labels and parity-check outcomes across codes including five-qubit, Steane, Shor, and rotated surface codes.
main_result: A hierarchy of ideal syndrome-memory energy costs is established as a function of code structure, noise model, and measurement representation.
application_angle: The framework can guide low-power QEC controller and measurement design for scalable quantum processors.

title: Spin-to-polarization mapping with a coherent quantum dot-cavity receiver
abstract: Coherent light-matter interfaces controllably modifying the state of a photon upon interaction with a stationary qubit are a key resource for implementing deterministic entangling gates for optical quantum technologies. This requires a one-to-one mapping between the state of the scattered photon and that of the embedded qubit. Here, we present an experimental signature of such a bijection by leveraging the spin-induced Kerr rotation present in a low-noise charged quantum dot-micropillar cavity device. Through time-resolved polarization measurements, we project the electron spin to one of its eigenstates with $95\pm2\%$ fidelity with a single reflected photon detection, and follow the subsequent spin relaxation through the detection of a second reflected photon. We demonstrate that, after a transient regime governed by the trion radiative lifetime, two orthogonal polarization states can be produced, each associated to a given spin eigenstate. While the current results are limited by a timescale competition between electron spin relaxation and trion radiative lifetime, they could be improved using hole spins displaying increased relaxation times. Our work paves the way towards deterministic logic gates exploiting this one-to-one mapping between a spin and the polarization of a scattered photon.
one_liner: A charged quantum dot in a micropillar cavity maps spin eigenstates onto reflected-photon polarization with high single-photon readout fidelity.
why_it_matters: Spin-dependent photon scattering is a core ingredient for deterministic optical gates and spin-photon quantum networking.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses a low-noise charged quantum dot-micropillar cavity where the embedded electron spin induces Kerr rotation on reflected photons. Time-resolved polarization measurements project the spin onto an eigenstate with 95 +/- 2 percent fidelity from one detected reflected photon, then monitor relaxation with a second photon. After a trion-lifetime transient, the device produces two orthogonal polarization states associated with the two spin eigenstates, although current performance is limited by spin relaxation versus trion radiative lifetime.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates a near-bijective spin-to-polarization scattering signature with 95 percent single-photon spin-projection fidelity.
application_angle: Improved spin lifetimes could make this interface useful for deterministic photonic logic gates and quantum-network nodes.

title: Ultra-Precise Quantum Projective Designs in Constant Depth
abstract: Random quantum objects are powerful resources for quantum information processing, yet exact Haar randomness is costly and typically unnecessary. We introduce an explicit sparse commuting circuit ensemble on $n$ qubits that reproduces low-order Haar moments in the stringent relative-error sense. The circuit consists of a sparse Clifford phase layer followed by independent single-qubit Clifford gates. Acting on a simple product state, the resulting ensemble forms $ε$-approximate projective $2$- and $3$-designs in relative error, with the required logarithmic interaction degree being asymptotically optimal within this circuit family. It admits an ancilla-free implementation of quantum depth $O(\log(n/ε))$ on an all-to-all architecture, as well as an adaptive constant-depth implementation---in fact, depth seven---using $O(n\log(n/ε))$ ancilla qubits. Departing from existing shallow-design paradigms, our analysis exploits the intrinsic moment structure of commuting phase circuits; at third order, this requires a new block decomposition and combinatorial analysis that also suggests a route toward higher-order shallow designs. Our results show that precise Haar-like statistics can emerge from sparse commuting dynamics with remarkably low quantum resources, with applications to randomized characterization, quantum metrology, quantum algorithms, and many-body physics.
one_liner: Sparse commuting circuits generate relative-error approximate quantum projective 2- and 3-designs at very low depth.
why_it_matters: Haar-like statistics with shallow, explicit circuits can reduce hardware cost for randomized characterization, metrology, and algorithms.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs an explicit sparse commuting circuit ensemble made from a sparse Clifford phase layer followed by independent single-qubit Clifford gates. Acting on a product state, the ensemble forms relative-error approximate projective 2- and 3-designs with logarithmic interaction degree, claimed asymptotically optimal within the family. It supports depth O(log(n/epsilon)) without ancillas on all-to-all hardware, or adaptive depth seven using O(n log(n/epsilon)) ancillas.
main_result: Ultra-precise projective 2- and 3-designs are achieved with logarithmic or adaptive constant quantum depth.
application_angle: The construction is relevant to hardware-efficient benchmarking, randomized measurements, quantum metrology protocols, and shallow algorithmic primitives.

title: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers electron spin as a quantum coherence probe of angular fluctuations
abstract: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers rare-earth ions combine giant longitudinal g-factors with a vanishing transverse component imposed by time-reversal symmetry, a combination that makes their spin transitions exquisitely sensitive to the orientation of the applied magnetic field. We show that this sensitivity carries a dual identity: it is simultaneously an overlooked decoherence channel and the basis for a spin-coherence-based angular probe. Using pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance at X-band, we report the first measurements of the quantum coherence of Tb$^{3+}$ in a native-doped CaWO$_4$ crystal (15 ppb) and map the Hahn-echo coherence time $T_2$ as a function of temperature (2 to 10 K) and resonant field ($10^3$ to $10^4$ G). A parameter-free model combining spin-lattice relaxation, instantaneous diffusion and spectral diffusion from all independently quantified impurities overestimates $T_2$ by an order of magnitude at low temperature and wrongly predicts the field dependence of $T_2$, inconsistent with the observed monotonic decrease of $T_2$ with $B_r$. A two-parameter extension, including dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis, reproduces the full dataset across multiple setups and laboratories. Two controlled experiments nominally identical except for different mechanical configuration of the setup establish the mechanical origin of the dominant contribution. The two-parameter extension corresponds to an angular amplitude noise spectral density of overall order 36 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ from global external vibrations (ranging from 10 to 66 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ depending on the exact setup mechanical configuration) estimated at $\sim$ 2.5 kHz plus a temperature-dependent contribution assumed to come from local phonon-driven angular jitter. It identifies and highlights a decoherence pathway of practical relevance to any anisotropic solid-state spin system.
one_liner: Tb3+ spins in CaWO4 expose angular vibration noise as a dominant decoherence channel and a nanoscale angular sensing mechanism.
why_it_matters: Strong anisotropic rare-earth spins can act as sensitive probes of mechanical angular noise that may limit solid-state quantum hardware coherence.
detailed_summary: The work reports pulsed X-band EPR measurements of native-doped Tb3+ in CaWO4 at 15 ppb, mapping Hahn-echo T2 from 2 to 10 K and 10^3 to 10^4 G. Standard impurity, spin-lattice, instantaneous-diffusion, and spectral-diffusion modeling fails by about an order of magnitude and predicts the wrong field trend. Adding dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis fits data across setups and laboratories, with vibration-linked angular noise around tens of ndeg/sqrt(Hz).
main_result: A two-parameter angular-fluctuation model explains the observed T2 limits and field dependence in strongly anisotropic non-Kramers spins.
application_angle: The result turns an unwanted coherence loss mechanism into a practical diagnostic for mechanical angular noise in anisotropic spin devices.

title: Algebraic Operator Decomposition: A Partitioned Architecture for Noise-Resilient Quantum Computing
abstract: We present an operator-decomposition architecture that mathematically maps a global operator into independently executable local operators, reducing the maximum quantum circuit depth at the cost of classical reconstruction and sampling overhead. By framing complex Quantum Circuits around an operator in a vector space that can be algebraically pre-decomposed, AOD complements quantum error correction and error-mitigation approaches by performing algebraic decomposition before quantum execution. Our approach leans in the computer science definition of a Monoid: a design pattern and mathematical concept consisting of a data type, a combining function that is associative, and a safe identity (neutral) element that does not change other values when combined. Simulation wise we define a MapReduce programming model where the addition (+) is the reducer, thus leveraging a naturally stable commutative monoid which carries zero "negative-probability tax" or phase conflicts. Furthermore, we define a Vector Space of Linear Operators over Additive Abelian Groups that benefit from this paradigm, including: Inner Products, Series expansions, Traces and Convolutions. Finally, we present the mathematical foundations and simulation results for this paradigm.
one_liner: Algebraic Operator Decomposition partitions global quantum operators into shallower local executions with classical reconstruction overhead.
why_it_matters: Circuit-depth reduction is directly relevant to near-term noisy quantum processors, though the proposal appears primarily architectural and simulation-based.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes decomposing global operators into independently executable local operators before quantum execution. It frames the reconstruction as a MapReduce-style additive monoid, aiming to avoid negative-probability or phase-conflict overheads. The claimed scope includes inner products, series expansions, traces, and convolutions, supported by mathematical foundations and simulations rather than a hardware demonstration.
main_result: The authors present an algebraic partitioning method that reduces maximum quantum circuit depth at the cost of sampling and classical postprocessing.
application_angle: If validated on hardware-relevant workloads, the approach could help execute larger algorithms on devices limited by coherence time and gate depth.

title: Frequency-Multiplexed Parallel Gates for Quantum LDPC Codes in a Two-Dimensional Ion Crystal
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes admit high encoding rates but require nonlocal entangling gates for syndrome measurement. Instead of physically moving the qubits which slows down with the increasing qubit number, here we propose to achieve parallel nonlocal entangling gates on a two-dimensional (2D) ion crystal using frequency-multiplexing. Adiabatic conditions ensure the suppression of gate infidelity and crosstalk error, as well as their robustness against slow drift in the trap frequency which is a leading error source in ion trap. We consider a numerical example of a $[[248,10,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code on a 2D crystal of 512 ions. By optimizing the mapping of the qubits and the assignment of the frequency bands for multiplexing, we show that a moderate laser power is sufficient for parallelism, and that a logical error rate of $10^{-12}$ can be achieved under realistic noise parameters.
one_liner: Frequency-multiplexed gates are proposed to run parallel nonlocal qLDPC checks in a 2D trapped-ion crystal.
why_it_matters: It targets a major trapped-ion scaling bottleneck: implementing nonlocal stabilizer measurements for high-rate qLDPC codes without shuttling ions.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes using frequency-multiplexed laser drives to implement parallel nonlocal entangling gates in a two-dimensional ion crystal. Adiabatic conditions are used to suppress infidelity, crosstalk, and sensitivity to slow trap-frequency drift. A numerical study maps a [[248,10,18]] bivariate bicycle code onto 512 ions and optimizes qubit placement and frequency-band assignments.
main_result: Simulations indicate that parallel qLDPC syndrome gates could reach a logical error rate of 10^-12 under realistic noise assumptions with moderate laser power.
application_angle: The architecture could make high-rate qLDPC error correction more practical for trapped-ion quantum computers by reducing syndrome-measurement latency.

title: Gravitationally Induced Entanglement Across an Event Horizon
abstract: It has long been assumed that a particle---having crossed a black hole event horizon unentangled with another particle in the exterior universe---can no longer dynamically entangle with that particle. Here, we demonstrate within a gravitational retarded-potential model that entanglement can in fact be created from scratch between freely falling spatial superpositions across an event horizon. Yet, extracting this state radially requires non-inertial deceleration, triggering soft-graviton bremsstrahlung, and establishing a strict dephasing bound in terms of entangling phase, $Γ\ge\frac{729}{160π}Φ$. This decoheres the entangled state. By contrast, equivalent macroscopic optical masses allow local tangential harvesting of entanglement via quantum erasure, thus revealing a remarkable geometric duality: Spacetime irreversibly degrades entanglement the moment the localized mass is dragged away from the horizon, while allowing the transverse teleportation of its entangled state to infinity.
one_liner: A gravitational retarded-potential model predicts event-horizon-crossing entanglement generation with extraction-limited dephasing.
why_it_matters: The result is conceptually relevant to quantum communication and gravity, but its application relevance is mostly foundational rather than near-term experimental.
detailed_summary: The paper argues that freely falling spatial superpositions can become entangled across a black hole event horizon within a gravitational retarded-potential model. It then shows that radial extraction requires non-inertial deceleration, producing soft-graviton bremsstrahlung and a dephasing bound proportional to the entangling phase. A proposed tangential harvesting route using macroscopic optical masses and quantum erasure avoids the same radial extraction penalty.
platform_or_system: spatial mass superpositions near an event horizon
main_result: The model predicts cross-horizon entanglement generation but imposes a strict dephasing bound on radial extraction of the state.
application_angle: It informs limits and possible geometries for quantum-information protocols in relativistic or strong-gravity settings.

title: Quantum thermalization achieves optimal approximate quantum error correction
abstract: Quantum thermalization explains how an isolated many-body system naturally evolves towards a thermal state, rendering information about the initial conditions inaccessible to local measurements. This is precisely the mechanism utilized in quantum error correction, where information is protected by design through a nonlocal encoding. In this work, we leverage this connection to port the rigorous framework of (approximate) quantum error correction to the study of quantum thermalization. Treating typical late-time states as codewords, we characterize the error-correcting properties of generic thermalizing dynamics. We numerically uncover a universal relationship between the encoding rate, distance, and thermal entropy density of the emergent code. At infinite temperature, this universal curve saturates the quantum Singleton bound, achieving the same optimal limit as Haar-random codes. At finite temperature, we introduce a code family based on the Scrooge ensemble, the natural thermal analogue of the Haar ensemble, and prove it saturates the entropic quantum Singleton bound, establishing this family as optimal within entropic constraints. Our extracted universal curve independently saturates this same bound, revealing that finite-temperature thermalization is itself optimal. Finally, we show how conserved quantities limit the error-correcting behavior of thermalization: codewords with differing energies, or other conserved charges, leak only classical information, and correctability persists until the difference reaches the scale of thermal fluctuations. Our results reveal a universal optimal coding structure in thermalizing dynamics, while introducing new optimal codes that achieve fundamental limits of approximate quantum error correction.
one_liner: Thermalizing many-body dynamics are shown to realize optimal approximate quantum error-correcting code structure.
why_it_matters: It links natural many-body scrambling to optimal code bounds, which may guide passive or Hamiltonian-based quantum memory designs.
detailed_summary: The work treats typical late-time states of thermalizing many-body systems as codewords and analyzes their approximate quantum error-correcting properties. Numerics reveal a universal relation between encoding rate, distance, and thermal entropy density, saturating the quantum Singleton bound at infinite temperature. At finite temperature, a Scrooge-ensemble code family is introduced and proven to saturate the entropic Singleton bound, while conserved quantities are shown to leak only classical information until charge differences reach thermal-fluctuation scales.
main_result: Generic thermalization is argued to produce approximate quantum codes that saturate optimal entropic bounds under broad conditions.
application_angle: The framework may help design hardware-native protection schemes that exploit natural scrambling instead of fully engineered code circuits.

title: Twin-photon generation in a silicon nitride microresonator
abstract: Photonic chips with silicon nitride ($\mathrm{Si_3N_4}$) microring resonators are well established as heralded single-photon sources, but their operation as frequency-degenerate twin-photon sources has not previously been demonstrated. Here, we realise a twin-photon source at telecommunication wavelengths in a $\mathrm{Si_3N_4}$ ring microresonator via an inverse four-wave mixing (FWM) process, in which two photons from spectrally distinct pumps are converted into a pair of identical twin photons. The measurements show a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio (CAR) of $5.4\pm0.6$. In addition, the microresonator functions as a heralded single-photon source through pump-degenerate spontaneous four-wave mixing (SFWM), exhibiting a spectral purity of $P=0.67\pm0.05$ and a heralded anti-bunching of $g^{(2)}_h(0)=0.0042\pm0.0015$. Together, these results demonstrate both photon-generation schemes on a single integrated $\mathrm{Si_3N_4}$ platform, highlighting its potential for scalable, tailored quantum light generation.
one_liner: A silicon nitride microring generates telecom twin photons and also operates as a high-quality heralded single-photon source.
why_it_matters: Showing degenerate twin-photon and heralded single-photon generation on one Si3N4 chip supports scalable integrated quantum photonics.
detailed_summary: The experiment demonstrates frequency-degenerate twin-photon generation at telecommunication wavelengths in a Si3N4 ring microresonator using inverse four-wave mixing with two distinct pumps. The source reaches a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of 5.4 +/- 0.6. The same resonator also functions as a pump-degenerate SFWM heralded single-photon source with spectral purity 0.67 +/- 0.05 and heralded antibunching g_h^(2)(0)=0.0042 +/- 0.0015.
main_result: The chip demonstrates both telecom twin-photon generation and heralded single-photon emission on a single silicon nitride microresonator platform.
application_angle: The platform is relevant for integrated quantum light sources in photonic quantum computing, networking, and telecom-band quantum communication.

title: Quantum communication and Bell nonlocality require infinite classical communication to simulate
abstract: A quantum system of any fixed dimension can be prepared in a continuum of states, yet it cannot be used to transmit an unlimited amount of classical information. Similarly, the correlations observed between measurement outcomes on separate parts of a shared quantum system can be stronger than classical correlations, but they cannot transmit information. These fundamental limitations suggest that the statistics observed from quantum communication and quantum correlations may admit a simulation using a finite amount of classical communication. This expectation is confirmed in the smallest nontrivial quantum dimension, with two classical bits being necessary and sufficient to exactly simulate qubit communication and all correlations between qubits. Despite significant efforts during the previous decades, this remained the only solved case. Here we resolve both problems for every quantum dimension. The solution reveals an unexpected qualitative transition starting at dimension four: no finite amount of classical communication can exactly simulate ququart communication nor all quantum correlations of two entangled ququarts, even with unlimited shared randomness. One might have expected this transition, if it existed, to appear already for qutrits. Instead, we construct an explicit protocol that exactly simulates qutrit communication using $357$ classical bits, and consequently, all correlations of two entangled qutrits.
one_liner: Shows that exact classical simulation of quantum communication becomes impossible with finite communication from dimension four onward.
why_it_matters: It sharpens the resource gap between classical and quantum communication, identifying ququarts as the first dimension with an infinite exact-simulation cost.
detailed_summary: The work resolves exact classical simulation costs for finite-dimensional quantum communication and bipartite quantum correlations. It proves a qualitative transition at dimension four: ququart communication and entangled-ququart correlations cannot be exactly simulated with any finite classical communication, even with unlimited shared randomness. In contrast, it constructs an explicit exact qutrit-communication simulation using 357 classical bits, extending the known qubit result.
main_result: Exact simulation needs unbounded classical communication for dimension four and above, while qutrit communication admits a 357-bit exact protocol.
application_angle: The result gives rigorous limits for classical emulation of quantum links and benchmarks where genuinely quantum communication resources become unavoidable.

title: Development of quantum technologies for optical/infrared interferometry
abstract: Quantum technologies may revolutionize optical interferometry through new means to distribute and preserve electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. After reviewing existing techniques, I survey proposed quantum-sensing and quantum-networking applications and highlight recent laboratory demonstrations of key building blocks. By easing field-transport demands for baselines beyond $\sim$1 km, quantum-enhanced interferometry could enable sub-milliarcsecond imaging and microarcsecond-class differential astrometry. That said, "going quantum" is not a magic shortcut to sensitivity because many of the most compelling science cases remain photon- and turbulence-limited. I therefore emphasize the practical constraints -- loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength limits of quantum interfaces -- that must also be overcome to make these capabilities useful for astronomy, whether deployed on the ground or from space.
one_liner: Surveys quantum-network and sensing technologies that could extend optical/infrared astronomical interferometry beyond kilometer baselines.
why_it_matters: It connects laboratory quantum hardware progress to concrete astronomy constraints such as loss, bandwidth, coherence, synchronization, and turbulence.
detailed_summary: This review evaluates quantum technologies for preserving optical electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. It emphasizes quantum memories, interfaces, networking concepts, and sensing protocols as possible enablers for sub-milliarcsecond imaging and microarcsecond differential astrometry. The paper is application-focused, stressing that photon flux, atmospheric turbulence, loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength conversion remain central barriers.
main_result: The article maps quantum-sensing and quantum-networking building blocks onto the requirements of long-baseline optical/infrared interferometry.
application_angle: It provides a practical roadmap for when quantum hardware could reduce field-transport demands in astronomical imaging and astrometry.

title: p-Adic Dirac Equations, Continuous-Time Quantum Walks, and Quantum Networks
abstract: We introduce a new class of p-adic Dirac equations, formulated in the standard axiomatic framework of quantum mechanics, in which the ordinary spatial derivatives are replaced by non-local operators built from arbitrary integrable kernels. We diagonalize the resulting free Dirac Hamiltonian in momentum space, construct its plane-wave solutions, determine its spectrum, and establish a p-adic charge-conjugation symmetry relating particle and antiparticle sectors. We then discretize the free equation in two ways, both giving genuine continuous-time quantum walks rather than the discrete-time, coined walks that dominate the existing literature: a first construction on a countable covering of the underlying p-adic space, and a second, more explicit construction on a finite, tree-structured graph, for which we prove that the transition probabilities, once the internal (particle/antiparticle) components of the wavefunction are combined, form a genuine, properly normalized set of transition probabilities at every instant of time; in other words, ignoring the internal structure of the walk, it behaves exactly like an ordinary random walk on that graph. Building on this stochastic-matrix property, we discuss how the resulting construction can serve as the foundation of a quantum network with genuinely relativistic-type internal degrees of freedom, complementing earlier, non-relativistic p-adic quantum neural networks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first continuous-time quantum walk whose free dynamics coincides exactly with a Dirac equation on a hierarchical graph. We close with a discussion of the open mathematical and computational problems raised by this construction.
one_liner: Introduces p-adic Dirac dynamics that generate continuous-time quantum walks on hierarchical graphs for quantum-network models.
why_it_matters: It offers a mathematically controlled route to quantum walks with relativistic-type internal degrees of freedom on tree-like network structures.
detailed_summary: The paper defines p-adic Dirac equations by replacing ordinary spatial derivatives with nonlocal kernel-based operators within standard quantum mechanics. It diagonalizes the free Hamiltonian, derives plane-wave solutions and spectra, and establishes a particle-antiparticle charge-conjugation symmetry. Two discretizations yield continuous-time quantum walks, including a finite tree-graph construction whose combined internal-component probabilities are properly normalized like a classical random walk.
main_result: It constructs a continuous-time quantum walk whose free dynamics exactly matches a Dirac equation on a hierarchical graph.
application_angle: The framework could support quantum-network and quantum-information models where hierarchy, nonlocality, and internal relativistic-like states are useful design features.

title: Phase Independent Measurement of Weak Coherent Optical Signals
abstract: We develop a quantum sensing framework for the phase independent detection of weak coherent optical displacements based on SU(1,1) interferometry. Unlike conventional quantum measurement protocols that require prior knowledge of the signal phase and coherent homodyne detection, the proposed approach estimates the displacement magnitude independently of its phase. We show that, under ideal lossless conditions, a conventional SU(1,1) interferometer employing only total intensity detection saturates the quantum Cramer Rao bound for displacement magnitude estimation. We further derive the analytical expression of the quantum Cramer Rao bound and the sensitivity of the conventional SU(1,1) interferometer with total intensity detection and systematically investigate its performance in the presence of optical loss. The proposed phase-independent intensity detection scheme achieves comparable performance over experimentally relevant operating regimes while eliminating the need for local oscillators, phase locking, and quadrature tracking. These results establish SU(1,1) based intensity detection as a practical platform for phase independent quantum sensing.
one_liner: Proposes phase-independent weak coherent displacement sensing using SU(1,1) interferometry with total intensity detection.
why_it_matters: It removes local oscillators, phase locking, and quadrature tracking while retaining near-optimal sensitivity in relevant regimes.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a quantum-sensing framework for estimating the magnitude of weak coherent optical displacements without knowing the signal phase. Under ideal lossless conditions, a conventional SU(1,1) interferometer with total intensity detection saturates the quantum Cramer-Rao bound for displacement-magnitude estimation. It also derives analytic sensitivity and QCRB expressions and studies degradation under optical loss.
main_result: Total intensity detection in an SU(1,1) interferometer can achieve phase-independent displacement sensing, ideally saturating the QCRB.
application_angle: The scheme is experimentally attractive for weak-signal optical sensing because it avoids coherent homodyne infrastructure and active phase tracking.

title: Three-Photon and Hybrid Coherent-Fock Interference in a Two-Phase Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer
abstract: We present a unified theoretical analysis of three-photon quantum interference in a Six-Port Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (6p-MZI) constructed from two cascaded tritters, with two independent phase modulators placed between the tritter arms. We analytically derive the transfer matrix of the 6p-MZI and show how they organize into three symmetry classes, governed by the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) structure of the tritter and the conjugate relations. Furthermore, we analyze two input regimes: First, three indistinguishable single photons are injected into the tritter, and the output probability distributions $P_{[111]}$, $P_{[\{300\}]}$, and $P_{[\{210\}]}$ are derived as functions of the two relative phases $(φ_1, φ_2)$. At $φ_2 = 0$, the single-phase limit is recovered, which confirms 100\% visibility of the even-distribution fringe. Second, a hybrid coherent-Fock input $|α\rangle_1|α\rangle_2|1\rangle_3$ is analyzed via the density matrix formalism. The average photon number at each output port exhibits amplitude-dependent phase shifts. Our results establish the 6p-MZI as a programmable platform for tripartite quantum state manipulation and coherent amplitude sensing.
one_liner: Analyzes three-photon and coherent-Fock interference in a two-phase six-port Mach-Zehnder interferometer built from tritters.
why_it_matters: The six-port MZI provides a programmable multiport platform for tripartite state manipulation and phase-sensitive photonic sensing.
